Is it possible to build a portfolio that has a historical P&E ratio of less than 25%? I would guess that, if you were willing to pay a premium for a higher-yielding stock, you could do it. But how do you go about doing this? How do your portfolio's average PCE ratio match up with the average stock price? Is it just a matter of buying a stock that sells for $1.10 and holding on for another $100? Or is it a case of finding a company that's been trading for two or three times the price of its stocks' PX? A lot of my peers in finance are saying that the answer is 'no.'
I realize that a 25%-P/B ratio isn't much to ask for, but it is a lot to live up to.
So, I am interested in your thoughts on this. I'd like to be able to do this, even if my risk/return ratio is less desirable than say, the 10% to 25%.
Thanks!
UPDATE:
By definition of the P-E of a security, its P & E ratio should be less that its price. So, my question is whether I should buy a low P.E. stock and hold on to it for its higher P price, or buy an E.P. Stock and sell it at a lower price (say $80). I suppose the question I'm asking is, is there a better way to go? 
A: How to make your P and E ratios match? There are two ways to get a P to E Ratio of 20:1 or lower. First, buy the stocks that are trading at the highest P / E multiple. Second, use leverage to buy stocks at lower P prices. 
If you want to use a leveraged buy, simply buy $10 of stock at $5 or more and add $2 to the buy price each month. You can buy 1% of your stock for 1/100th of $0.05. This is the leverage ratio that I used to meet my PEP. The reason I use 1%/month is that that is how long it takes to reach 1%. You don't want this to happen fast. Generally, a company announces a stock split, or a split of its stock, when it is about to go public. It can be on a day-to-day basis, such as when a big company like Facebook goes public, but it also can happen on an annual basis. In other words, it can go up in price in the middle of a month, and then drop in value the next month.
For a while, the trend was to announce a break in a price range, so that investors could sell shares, at a lower price, before the stock is reported to the public and prices rise. That’s called a “split” in finance. But since the internet has made it easier and cheaper to trade shares directly from companies, many companies are now announcing splits for more than just the first day of trading. This is called an “announcement” or “breakout.”
A breakout is the last day an initial public offering of stock happens, often after a few days. An announcement is when the company goes live. There are a lot of things that can change a market’ s direction and a breaking out is a good way to get a reaction to a change in market direction. A split is often used as a way for a hedge fund to make money on its investment in an IPO, because they can sell their stock at the higher price. The company can also make more money in this way. For example, Google announced its Google Finance IPOs on October 30, 2010. They split the price from $38 to $39.90. If you were buying Google on the day they went public you would have lost money because the value would be lower. Google is worth a little over $500 billion today. When you split a share, you get to profit on your investment.

What is the best strategy? How can you make money from this market in a way that is not too risky?
I’ve been reading about the oil markets for some time, and I’m finally getting my hands on a copy of the famous “The Black Swan” by Nassim Taleb.
In it he says:
“The market is an invisible hand that moves prices. It is there for a reason, but it’s not easy to understand why.”
The author gives some examples of how the market works, such as the fact that if you buy a house in London it will cost more in New York than in Moscow, because of transportation costs, or that the price of a new car in America is higher than the one in Japan. The book also talks about how “the market for oil is very close to the markets of gold, silver, copper, food and oil futures. And this is why oil has always been so important for the world economy.” (p.6)

The list cost is the average price paid by the pharmaceutical company for each dose of generic equivalent of that drug; it does not include the high fixed price charged by a brand-name drug manufacturer for marketing a particular brand of drug to a specific patient.
For drugs that are approved in more than one country, and for drugs approved by regulators in other countries, prices are established by an international comparison of list prices of similar drugs. In the case of drugs with a list-price-based approval, these prices typically reflect the costs of manufacturing the drugs in the country of origin. For drugs not yet on the market, a similar process is used to establish prices for products that have not been marketed. Each country sets its own list of approved drugs, which is then compared with the prices in another country. Because the price of new drugs is much higher than the corresponding list costs, most countries use a discount of 10-20% to reflect their higher costs. Many countries apply a more generous discount to drugs of higher value or with longer duration of use. Prices are updated regularly, based on information received from pharmaceutical companies and other sources, to adjust prices to market forces. However, even if a country has not taken market action, its list pricing is still used for calculating reimbursement in countries where the new product is being marketed, including the United States. At present, there is no standard mechanism for pricing or reimbursing drugs based upon their generic equivalents. There is an important difference between dividend increases and share repurchases. Share repurchase programs are designed to give investors a return on their investment in a company. Dividend increases are not.
Dividends are paid out to stockholders in proportion to the value of their stock holdings. In other words, they are a reward for stock ownership. It is not uncommon for companies to pay a dividend to a stockholder who holds a small number of shares, such as one share per year. On the other hand, share sales are often used as a way to reward shareholders who have large holdings of stock. A dividend, as noted above, is paid to shareholders on the basis of the number and value, not the ownership, of a particular stock held by a shareholder. For this reason, dividends are typically paid in the form of cash, whereas share purchases are usually made by issuing new stock or by converting stock from a current dividend paying stock to cash. The purpose of share purchase programs is to provide shareholders with an incentive to buy shares of common stock, thereby increasing the stock price. (See Figure 1.)
This is also the reason why companies that have a large number (e.g., 10 or more) of outstanding shares may often consider purchasing their own stock rather than issuing dividends. This is because the cost of issuing a new dividend is usually more expensive than the costs of buying a block of new shares. As a result, companies with a significant number outstanding stock may be more likely to consider issuing their shares as part of an overall share program or share exchange program than to purchase their share holdings through dividend payments. However, because most companies tend to issue a fixed amount of dividends each year, and because stock prices are highly correlated with the price of corporate bonds, it is often more profitable to repurpose dividends to purchases of preferred stock (see Figure 2).
For example, a corporation may choose to use a portion of its current dividends for the purchase of newly issued shares in its preferred corporation. These shares are then converted into common shares and may then be issued as new preferred shares (often called “convertible preferreds”).
The convertible preference shares that a preferred company issues to its shareholders have the same rights as the shares issued to common shareholders. If the total amount of your deposit exceeds the limit, you will have to declare the excess on your federal tax return. Generally, if the amount deposited exceeds $10,500, the return is due on or before April 15 of each year. For example, a deposit of $20,600 in January would be due in April of that year; a $25,700 deposit in December would not be reported until April. If you have a large deposit, however, your financial institution may require that you make a second deposit to cover the difference. In this case, make sure you file an amended return to report the second check. This is called the "late filing penalty" and is not allowed if you did not make the original deposit within the time limit. Make sure your check is postmarked by the due date. Sometimes you can make up the balance by making another deposit as you go along. Be careful not to deposit more than you actually have in the account. There are two main reasons that companies issue stock instead of cash: (1) to avoid tax, and (2) as a hedge against inflation.
Because stock is tangible property, it can be sold or traded, unlike cash. It's worth much more when it's held in a bank, but less when you have it in your hand. 
To avoid having to pay taxes, companies can issue more stock than they need to cover their liabilities. The less stock they have to issue, the less they're subject to taxes. This is also known as "tax sheltering".
The second reason is to hedge inflation: when prices go up, many people are worried about their money being worth less. By issuing more of their stock, they are reducing the risk of inflation by keeping more money in their pocket, so it doesn't depreciate as much.

Corporates and their shareholders are liable for corporate tax under the Internal Revenue Code, 26 U.S.C. § 6672, for unpaid corporate taxes and penalties that are owed to the government. The Internal Revenue Code defines corporate taxable income as “the gross income of a corporation,” 26 CFR § 1.6001-1(b), and defines the term “gross income” as the “amounts received or accrued from whatever source during the taxable year. However, corporate income may be reduced by “deductions from gross receipts”. 26 C.F.R. 1 and 1A.
In addition, corporations are required to pay estimated taxes, known as statutory taxes. 26 U. S. C.§§ 3001, 3011. Corporate taxes are assessed at the corporate level, and corporate-level taxes may only be paid by corporations. A corporation’s
“gross receipts” are its net income, its taxable profits, minus the amount of deductions taken from its gross income. These deductions are the ordinary and necessary expenses of the corporation, such as wages, salaries,
expenses, interest, depreciation, etc. If the deductions exceed the net receipts of the corporation by more than the statutory tax, the excess is taxable to all shareholders. In the case of dividends, shareholders who received less than they paid are also liable. As a result, if a corporate entity is insolvent, all of its assets are taxable, including its shareholders’
dividends. To prevent a loss of corporate assets, taxpayers may use the provisions of 26 USCS §
404(a), which allows a taxpayer to claim a deduction for all or part of an item of income. Section 404(c) also allows taxpayers to offset their income against their tax liability. It is important to recognize that corporations have the same rights as other taxpayers, which include the right to sue for a refund of any tax or penalties, or the ability to challenge any action or determination of IRS. Taxpayers can also bring an action for the recovery of unpaid tax and other penalties by suing the Secretary of Treasury for recovery. For a contract to be a valid stock contract, there must be at least one stock trading contract. A stock trader can trade shares or warrants. Stock traders who trade stock in the open market (that is, without a market maker) are called "market makers."
Stock traders will also trade warrants, which are similar to stock shares but are not traded on a public market. They are issued by a company and are traded by the company's stock exchange. Investors can buy them and trade them against the warrants' underlying shares. In a swap, one company will issue the warrant to another company, and then the second company can sell it to an investor, who then can use the trade to take advantage of the difference in price between the original and new warrant. A CDS is not a contract. It is simply a way of providing exposure to a security or a product. The difference between a bond and a credit derivative is that a collateralized bond or CDS provides exposure for a fixed or variable amount of the underlying debt. For example, a company might issue a CDO to provide exposure on a commercial paper it issued to bondholders.
However, the collateral backing the CDOs is often not fixed, but rather may be based on the company’s underlying assets (such as a property or equipment), or on market values. A CDS allows an investor to take a position in a derivative (a contract to buy or sell an underlying security at a specific price) by buying the contract itself. These contracts can also be “leveraged,” in which case the risk of default is spread over many contracts, or they can be collateral-free, in the sense that the investor is completely protected.

The question you have is quite different from the question of price-induced demand. The question is, if you buy the stock, and the share price goes up, is the increase in the value of the shares you own a good thing? Or, more precisely, are the changes in value more or less than expected? This question has nothing to do with the fact that the number of shares outstanding is fixed.
It is possible that, in a given market, the change in share value is more than you expected. However, it is unlikely to be more. If you were to buy all your shares at $20, but the market price rises to $25, your increase is $3. So if there were only a few hundred shares in circulation, you would be forced to sell them to make up the difference. That would result in an increase of your share ownership of less then 0.1%.
If you don't want to lose any shares, then buy at the $5 price. You would only have to pay an additional $0.01% to cover the increased value. In practice, this is not much of a concern. Even if the prices rise, most people will be happy to have a little extra money in their pocket. They are not likely to complain, even if they lose a couple of dollars. And, when the markets fall, they will have no problem selling their shares and buying new ones at lower prices. 
As to the effect of inflation on share prices, inflation is a natural consequence of an economy growing. For a long time, prices would rise as a result of increased production, demand, or both. But as economies grew, so did prices for all goods and services. Thus, a rise in inflation, which is what many people mean by the rise of share values, results from an increasing number, not a rising value per share. There is no reason to think that an increased number per capita would lead to a greater increase per person in income. An increase, per unit of income, could just as easily be due to an income increase.

According to the McDonald’s balance sheets, total equity is defined as: Total assets less total liabilities. Total liabilities are defined in terms of stockholders’ equity (capital) plus other liabilities that are classified as interest or principal.
The total assets is the total value of the assets on hand plus the net asset value, minus the equity. The net assets value is derived from the balance of accounts and is equal to total net income less: depreciation, property, plant and equipment, goodwill, and other intangibles. It is also equal, in most cases, to net worth plus int’l reserves plus accounts receivable plus debt plus inventory. If there is a net short-term liability, that is, a liability that will be matured within the next six months, it is included in the asset category of “Other” and not included on the income statement as a loss. For example, if a customer owes you $100 and the loan is due on October 1, you could have a short term debt of $5,000 and net-of-interest of -$5. This is not a long-lived liability and does not represent a decline in your assets. On the other hand, the $10,100 that you owe to your bank for a loan that matures in six years is long term and represents a negative equity balance. A negative balance is indicated in a balance-sheet by a line labeled “Total Assets” (or “Equity”).

for a Mortgage Loan I’m going to assume you’re familiar with the Truth in Lending Act, which is the federal law that mandates that every loan, no matter how big or small, must have a disclosure of “material terms” and “disclosures of charges.” The Act gives consumers two choices. They can choose to pay the full amount of the loan (which is called a “100% loan”) or they can pay a set amount that includes a fee, known as the “finance charge,” and the interest rate. The finance charge is calculated based on the cost of funding the purchase, but it’s also supposed to reflect the amount the borrower would pay if he or she had borrowed from a bank or credit union.
A common misconception about the disclosure requirements of Truth In Lender disclosures is that the finance charges must be disclosed. TruthInLender.com, the website that offers the most accurate TruthinLend.org disclosures, clearly states that if you pay off your loan in full, you will not be required to disclose the financing fees. However, if the lender charges you a finance fee and you choose not to take it out of your paycheck, then you must disclose that fee. If the bank charges the fee or you don’t take the money out and pay it back, that’ll be a different story. Under the Act’ s definition of a material term, “the amount you owe is a part of what you are charged,” but “you may not choose a payment of less than the entire amount,” which means you may be charged a lesser amount than you would owe if there were no financing. So if a lender asks you to make a larger payment, and your payment is $50,000, it is an “amount you” charge. That’d be the same as if they said, for example, $100, 000. In that case, they are only asking you for $40,001. Of course, a lot of consumers are not aware of this, so the best way to protect yourself from being charged more than your “true” amount is to be very careful when you make your payments. I recommend paying your loans in smaller monthly payments, meaning if your monthly payment comes to $300, pay $250 each month and save yourself the $25 that you usually pay to the lenders. You’ve got more control over what’ an amount your lender is asking for.

A discount is an amount that a lender gives to a borrower in exchange for a higher interest rate. In the context of the negative interest rates, a discount can be seen as a fee for agreeing to pay a lower interest payment. The concept of discount was first introduced by the economist John Maynard Keynes in his book “The General Theory of Employment, Interest, and Money,” published in 1936.
In the book, Keynes argues that there are two ways in which banks can make money by charging interest on deposits: the first is by making interest-bearing loans to individuals and businesses. This is known as the “principal-plus-interest” method. Banks can do this by offering a loan with a fixed interest, but then charging an interest fee to the borrowers. As long as interest remains at the same rate, the banks are making money. However, if interest falls, then the bank loses money, as it must pay back the loans that it made. A second way is to charge a negative rate of interest. Negative interest is when the interest paid on a deposit is higher than the rate that would be paid if the deposit were held to maturity. For example, suppose a bank charges a 9% interest for its deposits. If the deposits are held for 3 months, they will earn a rate in excess of 9%, and thus the fees paid to depositors. But if they are kept in a savings account for 5 years, it will take the money that was originally earned from the 9 percent interest to earn the 5 percent rate on the savings. Thus, negative rates of deposit interest are an effective way for banks to make a profit. It is important to note that the profit earned is earned by paying the depositor less than what would have been earned if all the deposited funds had been kept to be earned. Positive rates are simply different names for the amounts that banks charge depositing deposits, with no negative sign.

The United States Fair tax is a tax on the profits of businesses. It is levied on businesses which have an annual income of $500,000 or more in any of the fifty states.
In addition, the United State Fair Income Tax is imposed on corporations that have more than $25 million in profits. In addition to the income tax, corporations are also subject to a corporation excise tax. The amount of corporation taxes paid by a business depends on their annual revenue. For example, a company that has a $2 million annual business income can be taxed on a maximum of 5% of that income. If the company has $20 million of annual sales, however, they can pay no more taxes than 3%.
With the introduction of tax reform in 2017, Congress added a deduction for the fair tax for individuals, which means that the amount a taxpayer is taxed is reduced. There is no deduction if the individual is in a higher tax bracket and the deduction is doubled if they are in an additional tax brackets. This change is due to Congress passing a new tax code. Individuals with incomes of up to $200,500 are exempt from the tax and this includes the employer's share of taxes.

Income tax in the US is based upon a person’s federal income tax liability at the end of the tax year. The federal tax is computed by taking the current year’ tax and dividing it by the number of years the person has been in business. Thus, if the taxpayer had been a sole proprietor in 2015, the 2015 federal taxable income would be computed using the formula: (2015 taxable amount - 2015 taxable dollar amount) / (number of taxable years). In the case of a married couple, this calculation would include the combined taxable incomes of both spouses.
If you are a corporation, you can elect to report your taxable year-to-year income as either a pass-through or an installment method. A pass through is a method of accounting that is used when you pay yourself an amount on a regular basis, such as payroll taxes, and you then deduct that amount from your income. An installment is an accounting method that can be used to determine income for tax purposes based solely on the amount you have paid in, in advance, over a specific period of time. In general, a taxpayer must choose between an annual and a quarterly method to account for income in a particular year if they have a taxable period that begins in any given year and ends in another year, or if there is no end to the taxable periods. If you elect an installment, your tax will be based primarily on your “installments” rather than your total income, as the installments are based only upon the amounts you paid over the years. For example, suppose you’re a C corporation and your 2015 tax rate was 35%. If your installements for 2015 were $1,000, $2,500, $10,400, then you would report $16,800 in income and pay $5,600 in federal taxes. However, under an accrual method, income is reported on an ongoing basis and the reported amount of income will include any amount paid during the period. In the simplest terms, dividend payments are part of the cost of doing business for all businesses and companies. That includes you, the business owner. The business pays out the difference between the sale price of its product and the current market price.
This difference is known as a dividend, which can be paid out in one of two ways. You can have a regular dividend payment, or you can receive a special dividend. A regular or regular-plus dividend is the result of a merger or acquisition, where the company gets a new owner, takes a portion of that owner's stock, raises the capital needed for the merger, sells the stock and then pays the owner a share of profits from the new business. In other words, a company has no cash flow from it. It is then able to pay out a percentage of profit from its assets, known in the industry as the "dividend percentage." The new company in turn pays a proportion of this dividend to the rest of shareholders. This can mean the same thing as regular dividends in many cases, but sometimes it can also mean an additional payment. When this happens, it is called a "special dividend" or a bonus. If the payment is made by a stockholder, as is typical, then it will be known by the term "stock dividend."
A special or special-and-a-half dividend or "split dividend," as it's sometimes called, is a type of bonus, often called "bonus stock." It's paid to shareholders who have bought shares in a corporation in an effort to increase their ownership percentage. There are also special dividends paid by companies to their employees, who would otherwise receive regular salaries. These dividends are called salary or share-based payments. Sometimes, companies will pay a salary bonus to a particular employee, such as when that employee has been promoted to senior executive status. Or sometimes, they will take a lump sum, based on the number of years the employee or shareholder has worked for that company. They will also sometimes pay an amount to each shareholder, for a period of time, depending on how long the shareholder's service has lasted. Finally, some companies pay dividends to both current and retired employees. Such a payment will show up as both a base salary and a retirement benefit, with the amount being based upon the percentage in which the recipient's retirement benefits are invested in company stock. (See the next section for an explanation of retirement payments.)

The stock market is a complex and ever-changing beast. The stock markets can move in a whole range of different directions and, in the short-run, can go up, down or sideways.
On a longer-time horizon, the stock prices tend to move inversely to the growth of the economy. In other words, there is an inverse relationship between the rate of economic growth and the price of stocks. If the economic performance does not improve over time, then the market price may fall. On the other hand, if the same economic conditions persist over a long period of time and there are no major changes in policy, this may be good news for investors. While the long term trends of a stock’s price are not necessarily the best predictor of its short term movement, they can be used as an indicator of longterm trends. So, when stock values are rising, it is probably a good time to buy stocks, even if they are only moderately high. When they have been declining, you should sell. Stock prices, however, are highly volatile and you may not be able to predict how they will move. There is no guarantee that the move will be downwards, and it may even go in either direction. This volatility is one of many reasons why a person can make an emotional decision to invest in stocks and end up losing money. You should avoid being too emotionally invested in any investment. It is not the emotional investment that has made many people rich, but the rational investment decisions. Always remember that it’ll be up to you to decide when you want to sell and when to hold on to your investments. Investing can also be a risky business and should only be undertaken by those with a clear understanding of risk and how to manage it. Only by having an understanding and a plan of action can you be sure that you are getting your money’’back in time.

Is it possible to create a personal budget in Excel?
What does “double-end” mean in personal finances? 
A:
Double-ended is used to describe personal budgets.
Here's a simple example. If you wanted to build a budget for your family, you'd have a row for each of your kids and a column for the amount each kid spends per month. If, for example, your son's spending is $50 and your daughter's $100, then the bottom row would look like this: (Don't worry about the order, it doesn't matter.)
| | |
|
Joe | 50 | Joe Mary | 25 | Mary Martha | 20 | Martha George | 10 | George
 | 5 | George 
Don | 4 | Don
 | 1 | Don 
To build such a chart, first you create an empty chart. Then you make the first column a "header" and the last column the "footer" for that chart (that is, the row and column headers are reversed).
Next, create two new columns for columns A and B. Column A is the header and Column B is where you put the dollar amounts in those rows. For example: if you want your total spending to be $1,000, put a dollar sign ($) in the cell for column A, and put $0 in B (your spending column). Then, to fill that column, just add the sum of the columns. To make a total of $1000, add $500 in column B, $250 in A. (Notice that if the total is less than $5,500, use a negative sign (-) to indicate that amount is negative; otherwise, don't.) Finally, go to the chart tab, click the Fill Chart button, select the desired chart type (i.e. Bar Charts), and fill the entire chart with the data. You're done!

I think you are confusing "taxes paid" with "income" taxes. Income taxes are different from taxes you pay on income. I.E. if you were to pay the income taxes on a salary, and you had to use the money for something else, you would pay income tax on the salary. Taxes on wages, however, are not income, but rather a tax you must pay to the government. In other words, taxes pay for taxes, not for income or wages.
Also, I think your understanding of income is a little skewed. If you paid the 1040 tax return on your W-2 income (i.e. you got a refund), you do not pay any taxes in the US. However, if your employer paid you for the W4, the employer would also have to provide the IRS with the refund. The IRS would then have it split up between the 2 employees, one for 1041 and one 1042. For example, a $600 withdrawal would be counted as two transactions – $300 in your account and $150 in the bank. The $50 in each account would not be combined. As you note, withdrawing $20 in cash is not taxable, but withdrawing the equivalent of $10 in money (which is the amount that would have been deposited in an account) is taxable. This is why the deposit slips for withdrawals of more than $2,000 will indicate that the funds will have to be withdrawn in more transactions than the amounts shown in them. In this case, however, they will show the total withdrawal amount, including the second transaction in which the withdrawal occurred. It is important to note that, in most instances, only the first transaction is recorded on the original withdrawal slip. That is because, at the time that you make the transfer, your bank account is empty, and you don't yet know that your original deposit has been made. Once the account has a balance, this information can be recorded. Therefore, when you deposit $1,200, for example (that is, withdraw from your checking account $110 and deposit the remaining $980 in another account), it is treated as $900 in this example. But this is a different transaction than when $400 is withdrawn and deposited into the checking-account.

I have been asked to find the psychological barrier for a particular security and am wondering if anyone has had experience with this? It is likely to be a good example of a psychological or "moral" barrier that can be overcome in order to raise the value of the security.
Thanks Richard P.S. This is an example from the book "How To Buy Stocks: The Psychology of Security Prices" by A.Pichler, p. 23. (I can't post the full quote but it is about 40% of what is quoted.)
"Psychological barriers can also be used to explain market-clearing behavior. These barriers are particularly effective when they are internal, but can sometimes be external, too. The most common example is the tendency for investors to discount future earnings. As the market's price of stocks rises, the fear of future loss leads many investors in a high-risk strategy of selling early. When the price falls, however, many of these investors are likely not to sell at all, leading to a lack of liquidity. In effect, they have become trapped in the stock, unwilling to give it up. Similarly, if the earnings of an investment company are expected to grow over the next two or three years, then some investors will not sell stocks that have a value that is expected over that period. For example, in 1987, when the average price for American stocks was $20, most investors were willing to pay a premium of $3 or more for stocks with earnings growth rates over $2 a year. But when earnings started to decline in 1992, some would not have sold the stocks at $5 because they had expected the growth rate to remain stable at that level. If the company's earnings stopped growing, investors would have to wait to buy until earnings exceeded $6. And if earnings declined to $4, it would be too late to get in before the decline ended. So, while it may seem logical to assume that a stock is worth the premium it will command over a few years (given the expected growth), most people would rather not pay for the privilege."

Interest rates are a percentage rate of interest paid on the amount of money borrowed. Interest rates fluctuate because interest payments change over time.
The interest rate is the rate at which a lender pays interest. If the lender earns interest on a loan, the interest payment is called interest earned. The interest that the borrower pays on that loan is known as the loan's interest-payment. In a simple illustration, suppose that a bank loan a $100,000 loan to a business person with a 10 percent interest for a period of 10 years. That businessperson borrows $50,100. Assuming that interest is 10%, the bank pays $1,500 in interest to the business. This is $500 interest plus the $10,200 that is borrowed ($50 x 10%).
In a very simple example, if the monthly payment on an account balance is 100, and the deposit is 5 percent of the account's balance, then the annual interest charge is calculated as follows: 100 x (0.05) = $5.00. So the total interest charged is 0.5 x 100 = 50, which is 50 percent. Because the term loan means the sum of all interest charges paid, it is a misnomer to refer to interest as "interest paid."
When interest becomes payable, lenders charge interest by taking a certain percentage of what the money they loaned is worth. For example: If a company loans $25,600 to an individual, that individual may pay the company 10% of $20,400, for the next 10 year. At the end of this period, there is an outstanding debt of 25,800. Thus, each year, 10,700 interest will be paid to that company, plus an interest of 2,300 from the previous year's loan. A small business will usually pay a lower interest than a large business, because small businesses are often in the red and need to borrow more. As a result, interest starts at a higher rate than for large businesses.

If the option is "bought" (so the price is bid), then the buyer will need to pay for the stock at a price that is lower than the ask price. If the market price for that stock is higher than or equal to the current bid, then no price change will be needed.
You should not confuse "buying" with "purchased."
The option has been "sold" to you, so the seller has paid for it. The seller is willing to sell it to someone else at that price, but it is not going to happen, until some buyer agrees to buy at this price (or until the exchange period is over).
When the options are "offered" for sale, the only price changes that will take place are when the sellers will either accept a sale or decide to "sell" them to a buyer. In the latter case, they will immediately raise their price to match the new price of the contract. This is why the first time the trader buys an option at their ask, it will cost them nothing. They will have to wait a few days for a change in the "market" price before they can sell the contracts. Once the markets have settled, this will all be forgotten. (It's the same thing with the change on the offer, once the traders are out of that market, there will not be a "change" in price.)
Once the prices have been settled (which will likely take a couple of days), the buyers will start to accept new trades, and the newly accepted trades will then be added to any existing trades. Eventually, all the trades made will come down to one price - and then there is a single price at which all trades are accepted. When that happens, you will know that the next bid will go up, because the remaining buyers (who were not previously accepting trades at an ask) will accept the higher price as "normal." Then the selling price will increase, as the more buyers who have accepted it, will now accept it at its new higher market value. Finally, after the trading period has ended, when all buyers have gone through the process of accepting new bids, sellers should increase their offer price and buyers should accept. What is the Arizona state sales tax?
The Arizona State Sales Tax is based on the retail sales price of the item sold. The retail sale price is determined by the cost of all goods and services sold at the time of sale.
How does the state determine the sales taxes? The state determines the tax by taking the total of (a) the gross amount of taxable sales, and (b) any sales exemptions. This is done in the same manner as the federal government. Sales with a gross sales value of less than $1,000 are exempt from sales and use taxes. For example, a $25 item may be exempt if it is sold for less. A $10 item might not be, but if the seller is selling a taxable item for more than the $5 tax, then the excess of $2.50 is taxable. If the buyer wants the exemption, the purchaser must pay sales or use tax on that item. So, if you buy a car for $20, you pay $6 sales (exempt) and $8 sales. (Sales tax) If you sell the car to someone else, they must include the amount they paid for the sale in their taxable income. They have to report the value to the IRS and pay the entire tax. As a result of this, sellers do not want to sell to you, unless they pay all the taxes and sales plus the costs of doing business. In other words, buying a business is a taxing and selling business, so the best way to do business in Arizona is to pay your taxes on your purchases. That is why most people do it the way they do: they buy their supplies with their own money, or they use a credit card. It is very important that you know what you are buying, as it may affect your tax situation. Some items are not subject to sales taxation, including:
 Cash, checks, money orders, travelers checks and other negotiable instruments If you have questions about the use of tax exemptions, see the Tax Exemptions section in chapter 6 of our book. Also see our sales-tax exemption chart in part 1 of chapter 7.

I would like to focus on how a business can write-down good-will. Goodwill, when written down, is really just another way of saying that the company has not yet generated a profit for the year. That means that there is nothing left to be written-off. When the business takes a write off of good, that means there were never any profits made for that year, and therefore that company is not generating any cash for future years. A company could take this writeoff because the sales are not making good profits, the costs are too high, or the product is selling poorly. It is usually a bad time for a firm to do this because it is going to affect the firm's cash flow. The writeoffs have to happen when there isn't much to earn. If a cash-flow problem is holding up a new project, then the cash will not be coming in until the project is completed. In this case, it will be very difficult to get a project done, so the owners will write the down off good and then wait for cash to come in. They will also not take a loss on a job if they can't get it done. As a result, they will wait to see what happens with the new job before writing a down on it. Then, if a downturn comes, these firms will take the writedown because there will still be some profit coming from the previous year's sales. With this in mind, I would suggest that you not write any good off in the near future, because that will only delay the process of writing-offs. Instead, you should wait until you have a decent amount of cash coming into the bank. Make sure that it does not interfere with your current cash position. The first question you have to answer is: "Is your company taxed?"
If you are a sole proprietor, self-employed or a partnership, you don't have an obligation to pay any taxes.
However, if your business is taxed, the tax is a lien against your assets. This means your personal assets cannot be used to satisfy your debts. You can't just walk away from your house or business and start another one, because your tax lien will prevent you from doing so. 
For example, let's say you sell your home. Your tax liens are not paid off until your debt is paid. So you can no longer use the house to keep your current debt. (But you may be able to do so if you owe money on a loan that is being paid back).
It's similar for your car. If you buy a car and owe a debt on it, your taxes will stop you using the car to get to work. And if the debt has been paid, then you won't be allowed to sell it.

According to the Bank of Canada, Canadians pay an average of $13.64 per $100 of face value on their savings accounts.
That's a big difference. For example, in the U.S., a $1000 savings account with a balance of just $50 would cost you $1,500 to withdraw. It would take you three days. In Canada it would only take two days!
I can't find a direct answer to this question, but in 2007, the Canadian government announced that it was going to increase the minimum savings rate for every account from $5,000 to $10,0000. So, by 2008, Canadian banks would charge you an extra $500 per account for the privilege of using a savings plan. That's roughly the equivalent of paying $6,750 for a one-day withdrawal. (That sounds expensive, right?)
If you're wondering why the difference is so big, it's because the bank charges you fees when you transfer money from one account to another. There are three types of fees that banks charge: transaction fees, account fees and account management fees. Transaction fees are the most common, and are usually a flat fee of 1%.
Account management charges are fees paid to a bank for managing the accounts in a particular bank. The account-management fee is typically 2% of the total amount transferred. Other fees may include a 1% charge for transferring funds between Canadian and Usaan accounts, a 0.5% fee for transfers from Canadian to Uaaan, an additional 0% to transfer from Uaan to Canada and an 1.0% for international transfers. A 1+% transaction fee may be charged for online transfers, or if you have a debit card. Or, if the card has a 3% or more charge, you may have to pay a 2.9% fees for each additional charge. I'm not sure if that's the case for foreign cards, so check with your bank and see what they charge before you make the transfer. Some banks may charge a percentage of your transfer amount for any fees incurred during the transaction. You can also find information about fees in Canadian banking and transfer rates here.

This depends on how the stock is taxed. If dividends are taxed at the same rate as ordinary income, then you pay no tax. However, if the dividend is subject to a higher rate of tax, you will owe tax at that rate. The tax rate is based on your marginal tax bracket, so if you are in a lower bracket you may owe less tax than if your bracket is higher. For example, for someone in the 15% bracket your tax would be lower, because 15 percent is the marginal rate in this bracket. In general, dividends from lower tax brackets will be taxed less than dividends in higher tax rates. This is because the lower the bracket the less likely you have to pay tax to the government. Generally, the higher the percentage of your adjusted gross income (AGI) you make, and the more money you earn, your rate will go up. Therefore, as you get richer your dividends will also increase.

A bond is a fixed-rate debt instrument issued by a bank to a commercial borrower. It is issued for a specific period of time and usually is not redeemable.
Bonds are typically issued at a discount to the par value of the debt. Bonds can be issued to any commercial entity, but typically are issued only to companies with sufficient capital to repay the bonds. A bond that is redeemed at maturity is called a cash bond or a refundable bond. The term debonding refers to repurchasing a debt at the original maturity. Usually, a person or entity that repays a credit is referred to as a "repackager." A debonder is usually a company that buys a loan from a lender at any time during the term of a contract. However, if the contract is for more than one year, the debender is generally referred as the "repurchase" of that loan. This is done when the loan is maturing. In this case, there is no repurchase transaction. Rather, when a customer is repaid, they sell the bond to another company at par. For example, suppose the customer originally borrowed $100,000 in the first quarter of 2003, and the company repossessed the asset at $80,700 in March of 2004. If the $20,200 loan amount were repacked, this would be considered a refinancing of $50,100. Therefore, in this example the repackager would only repackage the old loan at an additional $10,600. Thus, it is important to note that when repacking a transaction, interest is calculated at 30% and not at 7%. While the answer to this question is still an open one, there are several reasons why it is advisible for investors to put a junk bond into their portfolio.
First, it might be advisiable for your portfolio to have some exposure to debt, as debt is a good indicator of future economic trends. This is because it has historically been a way of obtaining interest income and also of keeping a steady stream of cash in the economy. In this way, bonds are a great way for an investor to generate income in case of a downturn in an economy, and can also help a portfolio achieve a stable rate of return. Second, if you are going to invest in bonds, the key thing to remember is to diversify. If you put all of your savings into bonds from one country, you will end up with a low return on your money. On the other hand, by putting a portion of it into other countries, which have a more stable economy and thus higher interest rates, your return will be higher. The key is that your investments must be diversified. Third, debt has been known to provide an income stream for the long-term, while the interest on it can be paid off over time. Therefore, an investment in debt can help you achieve that goal of living comfortably, without having to worry about paying off a large portion every month. Finally, since interest is paid out in a predictable manner, a bank loan can provide you with steady income. And this is why people tend to choose debt in lieu of other investments. However, one must remember that a high-interest loan, like a car loan or a mortgage, can cost a lot of money over the years. So be sure to weigh your options carefully before making the decision to take out a loan.

They believe that if a stock is rising suddenly after reporting, it may be due to a change in outlook. There is an element of truth to this, but it's not the only reason stocks go up after earnings announcements. A company may have just reported a huge earnings result, and people think it will be a positive for the stock. It could be that the company is on the verge of announcing another big dividend. Or it could just be an inside trader who wants to take a quick profit before they have to report their earnings. Either way, the result is that you are getting a false signal. If you get a buy signal right before a close, don't be surprised if the price goes up. You should wait a little longer and buy when the real news comes out.

In a recent article, The Telegraph, I wrote about this question: How to Invest in the Coming Future.
Here's a summary: 
Investment decisions in times of economic uncertainty tend to be
 made with a risk aversion bias, which means that people tend not to protect their wealth in a time of uncertainty. People prefer to risk money, but the market is not a good place to do it. In times where the economy is doing well, people have a tendency to protect their wealth. This is because it is a hedge against future uncertainty,
thereby protecting them against a bear market. The opposite is true for a period of uncertain economic growth. As a result, there tends to be a strong bias for investors to invest in growth stocks, as they can take advantage of a better-than-average growth rate. 
 However, this is far from the only factor that influences investments. There is also an argument that the return of funds that are invested in higher-growth stocks over time is greater than that of funds that are invested more in lower-risk, lower growth investments. So even in good times, it's hard to find a safe investment. 
The article also discusses how the stock market and bond market are often very similar. You can buy a stock and sell it and it will outperform. Conversely, you can make a bond and you will lose money, if you buy it at a lower price than the bond is trading at. A common mistake that investors make is to buy bonds and then sell them. They think the bonds will go up in value and they can get a higher return than when they bought them, even though the underlying bond has declined. It's important to know that there is no such thing as a bond with unlimited potential. If you buy one and the price rises, then it is likely that you'll have to sell the same amount of that bond at a higher price to recoup your original investment, because the investment is worth more than what you paid for it, and your net income is now less.

If I rented a place for $2,000 a month on Airbnb and used the $1,500 as an investment for a start-up, would I be taxable on the interest? Or would it just be a personal interest because I was the landlord? 
A:
The short answer is yes, you will be taxed on all the income from the rental.
There are some exceptions to this rule. For instance, if you are renting the place to someone else and you don't own the apartment, or if the rent is below the threshold amount for that apartment. However, there is no limit on how much interest you can take. 
 
So if I buy a condo for my girlfriend in the summer for 5k, I can deduct all of the expenses related to the purchase of my condominium. If I take in $10,100 a year, this would be $5,400 in deductions. But if there are no expenses, it would just add up to $11,200 in interest. So the rule is that if we are not making any money from it, then we can't deduct it. We are just adding it to our income. There is also an exception for the investment. The investment is taxed at the same rate as ordinary income, unless it qualifies for an exemption.

The basic premise is that workers in a downturn are more likely to lose jobs than workers on a good job market because they are less likely than other workers to have the skills required for the job. And when jobs go away, they usually go to people who are already well established in their careers. To help workers get back on their feet, unemployment benefits are designed specifically to make sure that those who have lost jobs can still pay their bills. The program is also designed in such a way that people can have a second chance to get jobs if they can prove they have regained their skills. Why is commissioning a specific ETF more or less profitable than commission-free?
When you commission a certain ETF, you’re essentially paying a fee to the broker to get a piece of the investment. The broker is then free to spread the risk over a larger pool of investors, since he’s not being paid. But that doesn’t mean that he can charge whatever he likes. This is because he is in a better position to absorb the volatility of his investment, while the noncommissioned firm is less able to do so. In other words, if the portfolio of a free-of-fee firm goes up, the firm will be paid less for the same amount of money. For example, in the case of an ETF that’d charge a flat fee, it would be almost impossible for it to be profitable. Since it pays no fee for its services, its revenue is just a straight number. The reason why it is a bad idea is that when you invest your money in foreign securities, the value of your holdings of foreign assets fluctuates, and the net effect of that fluctuation is to increase your overall risk. By hedging your foreign exposure in the securities you purchase, or at least owning the underlying foreign stock, there is no fluctuation of value, so you do not need to worry about this. A portfolio of stocks that includes the currencies of all the countries in your region is the best way to make sure that you are not exposed to fluctuations in currency. International students
 
Credit is one of the most important factors in international students' decision to choose a school, and therefore, the credit of students. In order to obtain credit, students are required to have a credit report, or a record of their credit. For this, they need to get a copy of a report from their bank. If the report is available, then it is best to ask for a new report after the course of study, which will give you a better idea of your creditworthiness.
If you do not have the original report or the copy you can get from your bank, you should take the following steps to find a good source for your report:
 
 Look for the information about your account on the internet. This can be done by using the "Find My Money" feature of Google or by looking for an online report. You will find the account number and the bank's name. Once you have that information, go to the website of one the banks in your state and look for "My Accounts" section. There you will be able to see your history. 
 
 If you are not sure whether you need a re-credit report for study abroad or not, ask your academic advisor and/or the financial aid office. They can help you with this. It is also possible to request for credit after your study is done. The process of requesting credit is as follows: 
 Have an account in a bank that is related to your studies. Find the contact information of that bank on their website. Look up the address and phone number for their contact center. A. The future interest income to be received is not a new debt. It is merely the anticipated interest which the loan-holder is entitled to receive from the rental.
This answer is based on the assumption that the future income is related to the present income and that, because the second loan is a present loan, the income from it will be used for interest only and not for the principal. If this assumption is incorrect, then the answer would be “No.”
The future rent-receivable is simply a promise by the lender to pay the amount of rent at a future date. This promise is just as binding on both parties as the original promissory note. Both parties are bound by what the promisor promises and the promise can be enforced, but the payment of the promised amount can only occur when the other party has the money to do so. There is no present interest payment. Therefore, as with the interest paid on any other type of debt, interest on future payments is never included in the calculation of a debtor’s total debt to income ratio. Including it would distort the ratio and create a false picture of overall debt servicing. For this reason, future payment on a second-mortgage loan must be included as a part of total outstanding debt when calculating the debtor's debt service ratio with respect to a current mortgage.

The Future value of a deposit is the present value that it would have at the time of deposit. The Future return on a dollar of deposits is determined by the interest rate on the dollar and the return rate on deposits.
In this way, you can calculate the future value (future value) of your investments. There are two basic ways to calculate future values:
(1)
the discount rate and (2) the simple interest rate method. In both cases,
you can use the same formulas to get the Future values. If you want to know your future income, use either method to figure out your future interest. But if you have a large number of dollars to invest, the discount method is more convenient. Here is how to use it. We are going to assume that your annual income is $50,000 and your monthly expenses are $2,500. With this income and expenses, we are assuming a simple investment of $10,750. That is, assume the present value is 10, and that the expected annual return is 8%. In this example, $9,250 will be returned to you each year, or $11,650 total. So, your net future return will not be $1,550. Instead, it will have been $5,850. Now, let's calculate the remaining $350 by using the discounted future returns. This is called the Simple Interest Rate method, which is an easy way to estimate future returns. To determine the net future return, add the initial investment and any discounted future annual interest payment, then divide the total by $100, so you get $25.40. Finally, divide that number by 365, giving you an annual rate of 8.36%.
That is your Future Return, with an expected rate, 8% for the year.

The DJIAs are share price weighted because they have been used as a proxy for equity in the market.
When a company issues shares, the company has a stake in all the shares that are issued. This stake is known as the "equity". The equity is also known to be "weighted" (weighted stock market). So, for example, if a share of Apple's stock is 100 shares and it's worth $100, then it has an equity of $1,000. The share is worth 100% of the equity. 
However, a stock that is issued by a private company is not traded on the stock exchange. Instead, it is held by the shareholder. That means the owner of that share has no equity and the share can be sold at any time, at whatever price. If the price of a specific share rises, its owner will have to sell their shares to make up the difference. However, since the owners of stocks are not allowed to trade the stocks, they are forced to hold the investment in a bank or trust account. Therefore, these "private" shares are traded in "public" markets. These "stocks" are usually traded at a price that reflects the value of their equity, called "market capitalization".
Since these shares can only be traded publicly, when a large number of shares of stock are sold in one day, that means that the public market is over-weighted in favor of this particular company's shares. So the companies that issue shares have a "margin of safety" in their stock, which is the amount that they must hold in order to protect the shareholders from losses. For example: if Apple has 100, 000 shares outstanding, and they need to cover the $2,500 per share that a shareholder will pay, Apple will need $200, 00 to $300, 0 to buy back their own shares so that their share holders won't lose any money. A similar example would be a hedge fund.

In many states, the tax system is structured so that a business pays taxes on its income regardless of its state of incorporation, regardless whether it is a sole proprietorship or a partnership. For example, a corporation in California pays California state taxes, and a Texas corporation pays Texas state income taxes. However, it can be difficult for a small business to determine which state's tax law applies to its business.
The tax laws of all fifty states and Washington, D.C., are on the books. All states have their own corporate tax and income tax codes. Although it may seem confusing to decide which tax to pay, there are several ways to make this decision. The first way is to follow the state that has the most tax-friendly business law. If there is no state-specific tax code, then the best option is simply to select the business tax rate that is lowest. Another option, sometimes used, is called the "first-in, first-out" method. This is the method of selecting the lowest tax rates among all states. In this method, all the states are sorted into the order of their taxing rates. Then the smallest tax is selected for each state, which is then removed from the list. Next, each remaining state is moved to the top of the pile until no more states remain. These states with the highest tax are then moved down to their lowest rate until only one state remains. Therefore, for example if a company had two offices in New York, one in Manhattan and one at the bottom of Manhattan, New Jersey, California, Texas, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Ohio and so forth, this would result in the company paying the second-highest tax in each of those states—New York. The question here is whether the government should be lowering the interest rates on savings (and other forms of financial assets) in order to help the economy. In a recent NYT article, for example, the author argues that lowering interest on bank savings should help.
A:
 There are several reasons why the lower interest of the government could be an advantage for the economic situation. First, it would give more money to the people who are struggling. Second, there would be less interest on the capital the banks have to lend to other banks. Third,
there would less interest that the private banks would charge for depositing money. Fourth, more money would come into the banking system. 
 The interest reduction on deposits could help the banks by increasing the amount of money they have available to make loans. The government could lower the rates of interest for banks by giving them the money and the risk that they will have loans to make from the savings. In addition, lower rates for savings could encourage people to put money in the bank and not to use it to buy the goods and services that people need to survive. Lastly, lowering rates could help increase the demand for goods because they would have more money to spend. It could also encourage people to save more of their savings. 
Of course, such a policy would also have negative effects. For example: people could buy goods at a cheaper price. Also, in a situation where the rate of savings is low, people may not have enough to buy needed goods. This could cause inflation. And it could discourage saving. Therefore, to be effective, this policy should not be done by taxing people. Taxing savings would not reduce the overall demand for saving. Instead, a government can lower rates by giving money directly to people at lower amounts. They can also lower rates by making it easier for people
(and the companies that pay the bills) to get money from other sources. To do this, they could make banks and other financial institutions more attractive. Banks and financial institutions would have less trouble making money by selling loans that are not profitable. That would lead to more lending and more people would have money, and prices would fall, which would encourage saving and increase demand. All this would help reduce inflation and increase prosperity.

The world is not a zero-sum game. If there is a return to the shareholders, it is by the creation of new value. If it's not, then the return is simply a distribution of the value created by all the different players.
A:
 The world generates a positive return in two ways: 
There is an economic system that has some sort of positive feedback loop. For example, the price of a commodity is set by what it costs to buy, and the cost of production is determined by how much it cost to produce. This is the "supply and demand" model of economics. In this model, if there was a negative return, that would mean that the consumer was willing to pay more for the commodity than was needed to purchase it. So if the producer is charging a price that is higher than its costs, there would be a net negative gain for him, meaning that he would make more profit than the total cost. The producer would then be able to sell the excess to other buyers for more money than he had to invest in producing the product. And so on, ad infinitum. But the real world doesn't have a supply and a demand economy. It has a complex set of interactions between people, goods, services, etc. 
 There is also a cost-effective allocation of resources, such as the use of natural resources. Natural resources are often scarce, but are typically plentiful. As a result, natural resource use can have an enormous positive economic impact. (Think of what happens when you throw a rock into a pool of water, or what would happen if all of your money went into one of those little plastic buckets.) 
 
For example: We may be interested in how the resources of nature are used, because we are concerned about the effect that our use is having on the environment. We might want to know how to conserve natural energy. Some of our energy is produced by burning fuel such a coal or oil. Others of it comes from the sun. Our use has an impact on nature.

A stock is a measure of the value of a company in relation to its competitors. This is typically expressed as an index, with the index being a weighted average of all the stocks in the same industry.
 
The most common type of stock index is the S&P 500 index. The S &P is an industry index that tracks the performance of 500 of America's largest corporations. The 500 companies are divided into five industries: Industrials, Consumer Discretionary, Financial Services, Industrially-Focused, and Utilities. These five sectors are further divided based on their financial strength:
 Industrial
 Consumer discretionary
 Financial services
 Industrial
 Utilties Income stocks are a type that is not included in these five indexes. Income stocks typically have a higher price-to-earnings ratio than the other stocks, which makes them a lower investment. They tend to have less liquidity and tend not to be a highly publicized company. Additionally, it is difficult to find information on income stocks since their sales are generally less than a third of those of their peers. 
Many other types of indexes are also used. For example, the FTSE 100 Index tracks a group of 100 of Britain's biggest companies. It is considered the world's most important index of companies in finance, investment, insurance and technology. Similarly, many index funds track stocks of many of these sectors. Some of them are more specific, such as the U.S. Technology, Health Care, Energy, or Health stocks. A smaller number of index stocks focus on a specific industry, e.g. the American Express Index. 
An index does not need to track all of an economy's stocks to provide a good estimate of its performance. The capital gains tax is an important part of the equation. There are two components to the capital Gains tax:
Your tax bill will be lower if you have fewer shares than you would if your total holdings were larger. If your actual holding is smaller than the number of preferred and common shares you own, then the ACCGT will reduce your tax by a percentage of that number. This percentage is determined by your current stock price and the price at which you purchased the shares. So if the market price of a stock is $10, you might have to pay a 15% ACCG. But if it is currently trading for $4.00, that 15 percent is only worth 5 cents. Even though you may have $15 in preferred stock, the 15 cents you pay on that $5 is not worth the $2 you paid for the stock. Since this tax will only reduce the amount of capital you owe, it does not matter if there are fewer preferred or common than preferred. It will still have an impact on your overall tax. For example, if a company is reporting $100 in total assets, but $200 in capital, and you are the sole owner of $50 in common and $150 in preference shares, your effective tax rate would be 33%.
As for why preferred shareholders would want to have smaller holdings? Well, they do not pay income taxes, so there is no reason to own more shares if they are not in a position to make a return. Also, preferred ownership is a tax shelter – if shares are sold for less than their market value, there will not be any tax to be paid. However, these tax benefits come at a cost. With smaller preferred holdings, a person's taxable income will go up, even if he/she has no capital losses. As a result, people who are primarily in the business of making a living will probably want smaller numbers of common, rather than larger numbers. Of course, with the large number, common shareholders will lose out. While these differences may not seem significant, this is the difference between the two tax rates. And the higher tax burden is what drives the preference shareholders to want fewer holdings.

The first question is a little trickier. The way that high volume tends to indicate high volatility is not a one-to-one relationship. For example, if you have a $100 stock with a low volume of trading, but the volume is at a level that is considered high, that may not indicate that the stock is particularly volatile.
For example: if the average volume per trade is $10 and you see $1000 in volume, you might have high transaction volume. But if that volume rises to $20,000 and then declines to a volume that's considered low, it's not necessarily a sign that your stock has been volatile or that you should be concerned about the volatility. If you had $60,500 in transaction volumes, then you may be more concerned. In general, high volumes are a better indicator of high risk. You can have $1,300 in volumes and see that $30,200 of volume has traded. That's a large jump in trading activity, and it doesn't mean that that stock will be a volatile stock. It may mean, though, there was some sort of unusual event that caused the price to spike or fall. High volume may also indicate a lot of "pump and dump" activity. A stock that trades a ton of shares a day may have low volumes of trades, meaning that investors are trading at the same time, or there may simply be no volume at all. There are other factors that can affect high and low trading volumes as well. These are all factors to consider when looking at high or low transaction activity in your own stock portfolio. 
In short, volume and the number of transactions is only one of the indicators you can use to gauge the liquidity of a particular stock, which is why it can be misleading.

Q. Can you take an Oversea Earnings Deductible for foreign income? What if the foreign business is a non-U.S. corporation? A. Yes.
The issue here is whether the home-office deduction can be taken if a foreign corporation is the taxpayer's employer. The Commissioner has ruled that it can. See, e.g., T.C. Memo. 2003-80, 2003 WL 720628 (Oct. 6, 2002). However, the Commissioner is not bound by that ruling, and has allowed other taxpayers to take a deduction under the same circumstances. Id. at *4. In addition, although the OCI provides that a taxpayer may deduct the expenses of the corporation's foreign operations, this provision applies only when the person who is taxed on the basis of income derives his income from the U.K. or Ireland, not the Republic of Ireland. O.I.G. § 8-5(2)(c). Thus, if you are a Ulster-based taxpayer, you cannot deduct any of your overseas-earned income for the purpose of home ownership. You can, however, deduct your home expenses if your corporation has a physical presence in the UK. That being the case, it is clear that the income of a corporation that is subject to UCI will not be deductible under any circumstances, because the tax law does not permit a tax deduction for income that derives from a particular country. This is true regardless of whether such income is from home employment or from an overseas business. To the contrary, under current law, a person's home business income cannot be reduced by the amount of his overseas earned income. However if such a company is an Irish corporation, then the company's income can not only be claimed for home use, but also be subject the deduction provided in section 22 of OEI. Accordingly, in this case the plaintiff's deduction of $10,000 is reduced to $6,500.00.

The answer to this question is an emphatic yes. The IRS has long ago concluded that a sale or other disposition of property does not constitute a deduction if the disposition is made within a three-year period. It is a long-standing principle of statutory construction that an unambiguous statute must be given effect. See United States v. Alsup, 732 F.2d 1065, 1068 (11th Cir.1984) (citing United Savings Ass'n v, Timbers of Inwood Forest Associates, Ltd., 484 U.S. 365, 371-72, 108 S.Ct. 626, 630-31, 98 L.Ed. 2d 740 (1988)). The plain meaning of section 165(c) is clear and unambiguous: the sale must occur within the three years prior to the year in which the deduction is claimed.
This interpretation is further supported by the legislative history of the statute. In 1969, the House of Representatives Committee on Ways and Means explained that the section was enacted in order to "provide that taxpayers may use the accumulated depreciation method to reduce their federal income taxes on the value of their property...." H.R.Rep. No. 92-1380, 92nd Cong., 2nd Sess. (1969) reprinted in 1969 USTC ¶ 5159, at 5161 (emphasis added). The House report concluded:
It is not the purpose of this bill to allow a taxpayer to use a depreciable asset as a basis for the deprecation of an income tax deduction. Rather, it is the intent of Congress to require that only the actual acquisition of a capital asset be used as the basis of deprecding the income. A taxpayer is required to take into account the fact that depreceed property is depracted to determine the amount of income subject to tax. To allow the use of capital assets as depredation bases would be to permit taxpayers to obtain a substantial tax advantage by disregarding the real cost of acquisition. [emphasis supplied]
In other words, Congress intended that capital depersonalization be a means of reducing income rather than a method of eliminating income altogether. However, the crypto tax is a double taxation, so you pay both taxes, including the capital gains tax.
If you are investing in a crypto currency such as bitcoin, you do not pay capital-gains tax on the gains. This is because your gains are not realized until the next year, which is why you would not have to pay the taxes if you were holding it for the year. The capital gain tax you will have pay is on your profits for that year if they are realized within that one year period. Therefore, if your crypto portfolio is held for less than one full year you can have a higher tax savings than if it was held more than a year (and that’d be the case if the cryptocurrency you’re holding is volatile).
For example, let’ s say you hold Bitcoin for 1 year and you have $2,000 in your Bitcoin portfolio. If you sell it to a dealer for $3,100, they will get a $900 tax credit. That is the amount of the tax reduction on $1,300. So, that is $100 you get back. Now let us say the total value of your portfolio increases to $4,200. Since you sold it at $6,500, your total tax bill is now $300 ($6.500 - $5.200 = $150). This means you got a tax cut of $50. And this is only if, and when, Bitcoin goes up in price. (If it does, then it will be worth more in one-year. But this will not affect the calculation of tax-saving.)

Stock exchange listings are not "market-timed". Stock exchanges are "price-time", not market time. For example, if a company wants to sell 100,000 shares for $10 per share, it can do so on any day at any time, but it cannot decide how many shares to offer at that price until the day comes. The day that the stock trades at $12.50 is the "time" when the offer is made, not the moment when it makes the actual offer. Similarly, the time of the closing of a stock transaction is not a market-based "point in time" but the date that a transaction was actually completed. 
As another example: if the company announces it will buy back 100 shares at the price of $20 per, and then it sells them all for a total of 100+20=140 shares, that is a "stock-deal", but not because the market has "timetimed" it, or because it has determined it needs to buy the shares back, because that's not what the announcement is about. It is just a good business decision, based on its information, to do that. If it later decides to increase the number of shares it buys back from 140 to 200, then that would be a new stock-sale, though it would not be "a stock deal" because there is no "date in market" for the transaction.

This is because, for a fixed rate loan with a very low APR, the interest will be higher each year. You’ll have to make more payments each pay-off period. If you need to borrow more money to meet your monthly payments, then you can save by paying extra. In other words, by not paying off the loan early. To avoid this type mistake, check your APR to see if it is too high. Sometimes the best thing to do is to negotiate your loan terms to reduce the amount you pay per month. Most student loans have an annual percentage rate that can be reduced. For example, if your interest is $10,000 and your payment is at $1,500 per pay cycle, that’ would be $800 per year, which is less than the $2,100 you would pay in interest if the rate was 10%.
So, in a nutshell, save the lump amount each monthly payment, and save more as you make payments. However, this does not mean you won’t be paying any interest at all. There are many variables that affect the APR of the student-loan debt, such as the age of your student, how much money you owe, whether you want the money paid in full, or whether the payment will increase with each payment date. Some people choose to use the debt as a way to get a second job, so they can pay it back in less time, rather than pay the full amount off. Many people who are in school, with no job experience, have student debt to help pay for their education.
