What is a broker and why do they exist?
Brokerage is the practice of buying and selling securities. These securities are typically traded over the counter (OTC) and are called “securities.” Securities are traded for different types of investment purposes, including:
 To invest in stocks, bonds, mutual funds, and other investments, typically for a specified time period, such as one year or a set number of years.
Often, these investments are made with borrowed funds. Borrowed funds are borrowed from a bank or other financial institution, or they may be borrowed directly from the investor. In this case, the funds come from another person, who may not have a financial interest in the securities being purchased or sold. The investor pays a fee to the broker for the use of borrowed money to purchase securities, which are then sold to other investors. Sometimes, brokers are paid a commission for their services. For example, a salesperson may receive a percentage of a sale, as a finder’s fee. Investors can also pay a higher fee for broker services, in which case the fees are based on the size of the transaction. Brokers can charge a variety of fees. Some fees include: sales charges, commission fees, transaction costs (such as processing fees), and fees related to maintaining the accounts of investors (broker fees).
While brokerages are a common way for investors to invest, many investors are not satisfied with the investment they receive. They want to receive more returns, without the risk of having the amount of capital they invest reduced. If this were not the case for many, there would be no need for paid broker service. The asset prices of the world's largest companies are typically measured by the so-called beta. In the simplest terms, beta is the price of a stock divided by its expected future earnings, which is also known as the beta of earnings growth.
A beta above 1 indicates that the stock is more expensive than expected and is expected to rise in value over time. A beta below 1 is an asset that is considered cheap and expected value for the future. The asset price is typically the market capitalization of an investment company (a stock or a fund).
When it comes to the markets, a value above 0.8 is very high, and one value below 0 is a very low value. So, when it's time to sell, the value of your portfolio should be between 0 and 0,8. That's a pretty safe range to have in your asset portfolio. If your beta value is 1.0 or higher, then it may be time for a change in the portfolio, because you can expect to see a decline in future value in a rising market. On the other hand, if your value exceeds 1, it means that you may have a better chance of outperformance (overperformance) in an overvalued market, than you would in any other market environment. However, keep in mind that there are many other factors that affect your investment, including, but not limited to, government regulations, taxation, legal risks, market psychology, inflation, interest rates, etc. Your portfolio may not be the best fit for you, or it could be a good fit, depending on your risk tolerance, goals, objectives, risk profile, time horizon, investment history, tax status, geographic location, budget, current investments, family, age, health, personality, life goals and other things you consider important. It's also worth noting that beta can be affected by many factors outside of any one investor's control, such as geopolitical risks and political events.

If you buy a lot of the same stock, you can be sure that your broker is working for the bigger broker, so you get the best deal. This broker may also have other services, such as advice and research, that you may not be able to obtain from a more local firm or direct from an investor. If they make the profit, then you have a net gain on the investment, or you are making money off the investments. In the case of an individual, you can reininject shares by selling your own shares. You can also reinjure a share by buying shares for yourself. The question is, what is the current (net) value of the portfolio? 
Should I buy the stock back and start again? Or, should I just sell the whole portfolio and buy back some of it? What is an acceptable risk/reward ratio? Is there a formula I can use to find the correct answer? 
A:
While you could always buy another lot and re-invest it, you can't do that without selling it first. You have to sell it to get the net value. So the answer is: you should sell all of your stock and then buy it back. 
You don't want to have that much money in the market. If you do, your money is likely to become illiquid. That means that if you buy some shares of a company, they can go down in value quickly. And if they go up, so does your portfolio. So if the value goes up (or down) you have more money to invest and the more likely you are to make money.

There are two ways to do this. The first way is by purchasing stock in the company in which you hold a stock certificate. You can buy stock using the shares that you already own.
Once you have bought stock, you can sell it. If you sell the physical shares, the seller will give you the cash that is used to purchase the original shares. When you buy the new shares at the same price that they are selling for, then the buyer will sell you their original stock. This is called a reverse merger. (This is also known as a "split" in other markets.)
You can also buy shares of stock directly from the owner of that stock (the company) by buying the share of shares directly. Again, when you purchase that share, it will be sold at a lower price than the existing share price. That is known in stock finance terms as the "bid-ask spread". The bid-asked spread is the difference between the price of a share on the day of purchase and the current market price at that time. A higher bid will allow you to obtain a higher price for your shares than you would get from selling them at an "ask" price, and vice versa. In other words, if you were to sell your share at $10, on an ask basis, your bid would be $12 and your ask would pay $8. On the other hand, a buy-it-now basis (i.e. a market-bid) would allow a buyer to get a bid of $15, but the ask will pay only $11. Thus, with a sell-at-market-price (SMM) basis you could sell for $16 instead of paying $13. Similarly, buying a shares from a company is similar, except that the market will set the asking price and you will get the higher ask price instead. Once you own a physical share in a corporation, be it a private company or a public company, selling or buying it is straightforward. However, in most cases you must first purchase a certificate that can be used in order to exchange your physical certificate for a new one.

Technical analysis is a broad discipline that is concerned with trading and investing in stocks, bonds, commodities, currencies, and other financial instruments. It is based on the use of technical indicators, which are numerical measures that show the market's current state, or trend. Technical indicators have been developed to help traders make decisions about which stocks and bonds to buy or sell and which currencies to invest in.
The four main technical components of an indicator are:
Price: An indicator's price is the price of the stock or bond it is representing. A price above or below a particular point in time is an indication that the current price represents a change in the direction of a trend or in a current market condition. For example, a price below 1.00 is considered a sell signal, whereas a higher price indicates that a stock is trading in an uptrend. This signal is often used to indicate that buyers may be in control of prices. The price level should be compared to the previous level to determine the trend direction. Price levels are measured in terms of dollars, shares, cents, pence, yen, etc. where the unit is most relevant to a specific market or industry. 
Volume: Volume is how many shares of stock are available for trading, divided by the number of shares that were sold on a given day. Volume can be measured as a percentage, such as the percentage of total volume that was sold. When the volume is high, the stocks or bonds are more liquid than they were on previous days. However, when volume levels fall below 50%, the signal to sell is strong, as this indicates a market with less buying volume. If the same volume level is reached again, then the buy signal can become stronger. Volumes should also be considered when the indicator is compared with a historical average, since historically low volumes have a tendency to signal a strong trend, while higher volumes are usually a sign of low price activity.Volume is measured using units such a million shares or thousand shares. Calculate the difference in the two profit or loss numbers Determine which number is greater Multiply the number by the risk (in this case, the value of your delta) and add it to the current delta value Add the amount of delta to your position.
Note that you are not currently adding your risk. Your position has been created because you calculated a risk value. However, you may have a small amount left over. This is your buffer. You may need to add more to keep the buffer at $40 (you may want to use a calculator if this is a tricky question).
You can use this formula: delta = (profit - loss) * (risk - buffer) / (buffer + risk) where risk is the loss you would have if the market moves against your portfolio and buffer is whatever amount you want. In this example it is $15, because if it were $30, your initial $100 would be lost. If it was $200, it would not be. I think that’s a good question, but the short answer is that “benefit” is a more specific term and is used to describe pensions that pay based on a defined benefit formula. “Defined benefit pensions” are much broader than this, and they include defined contribution plans, defined-benefit-plus plans and other types of pension that aren't defined as benefit plans.
The key point about the difference between defined contributions and defined benefits is this: a pension plan that pays based only on defined amounts is called a “fixed-rate pension,” and a plan where a portion of the benefit is set aside for a designated beneficiary is known as a "defined-contribution plan." (I'm a relative novice in this subject, so I'm not sure of all the nuances here.)
In the case of defined pensions, there are two types: defined pension (the default) and guaranteed-defined pension. If the plan is defined, it has a fixed rate of return. Guaranteed-defined pensions are defined to a lesser degree, usually based not on the rate but on some other factor. For example, if the employer matches the employee's contributions, then that's a guaranteed pension, not a rate-of-return defined plan. This is also known by different names: guaranteed, guaranteed investment, or guaranteed benefit. In general, you can't switch plans or switch employers or anything like that, because the guarantee applies only to the defined amount. So if you switch jobs, your pension would change. A bond with a par amount of its yield may not be exactly worth that amount, but it may be worth a higher amount than the market price of the bond would indicate. If the coupon rates on a particular bond are higher than market rate, the bonds are discounted, while if the coupons are lower than or equal to market rates, they are not discounted. The difference between the two options is known as the par discount, which is often expressed in terms of percentage points.
For example, suppose the price on an MBS bond is $2.00 per share. Assuming that the interest rate is 5.5%, the discount rate for the $1.50 par bond might be 10%, or 0.10%. The coupon yield on this bond may vary from the 5% rate to 7.0%. If interest rates are low, bonds may command higher coupon yields than they should, because investors may fear that rates will rise. This is called a “risk premium.” For example: Suppose that at 5%, interest may rise to 6%, but at 7% interest is still at 6%. Market efficiency is the number of sellers who are able to deliver on an agreed price for a particular quantity of an asset. If the market is efficient then there will be no price disparity between buyers and sellers. The higher the liquidity, the more buyers will take part in the price formation. In a market in which the supply of the asset is limited, it will always be a buyer's market. On the other hand, if there is a lot of supply, sellers will have to compete with buyers for the limited supply. Therefore, there could be an excess of buyers compared with sellers and a price dispersion.
The price of a given asset will fluctuate in response to supply and demand in a free market, and will not be stable. Thus, an increase in liquidity will lead to an increased supply in order to maintain the prices. For example, a stock with a high level of liquidity could have a higher price than a security with little liquidity. When the stock is sold, some buyers may have excess liquidity than others, which could result in an oversupply of shares and decrease the value of that security. However, this overproduction of stock could also result from other buyers having excess supply compared to sellers, i.e. when a large number are shorted, they will sell at a lower price and have less to buy in comparison. This would result into a decrease in market liquidity to the extent that the available supply decreases. A decrease of market efficiency could occur when there are too few buyers to satisfy sellers compared that there would be too many buyers. It can be seen that a lack of excess demand and supply could lead the entire market to a liquidity crisis. There could even be the opposite situation, where the lack or excess availability could increase liquidity compared other situations. “Context” is a word I’ve used a lot. It’s a fancy way of saying: “the way you talk about money is the way people talk to you.”
This can be confusing. I think the key to understanding context is to first realize that context doesn’t matter. When you’re talking to someone you have an obligation to be polite, to act in a way that will be perceived as polite. But that doesn't mean that you can’ t talk as if you were talking about the money that they are paying you.
For example: If you are negotiating with a friend and you know that their company pays a salary, and they don’’ know how much you make, you don't have to tell them what you do for a living. You can just say, “I work for the company that pays me.” If they ask for more information, say something like, "I can't give you a dollar amount, but if I were to say that I make $250,000 a year, I would be lying."
The point is that the context does not matter, because context can influence how we think about what we do. We think that if we were paying someone $50, they would have more money than we have, so we can afford to pay them more than $5. Or we would think they were poor and we could afford them. This is just a fact of the world. So if a person pays you $100, we aren't going to assume they have $10, or $200, if that makes them feel bad. Instead, it’ll be easier for them to feel good about paying us $20. In other words, context has nothing to do with what people think we are worth, even if they think you're worth more. The context of what they pay you doesn'’ have anything to with the amount they feel they’d be willing to give. What would the consequences be of a rate hike? (What do you think they would do if they did?)
If the answer is "nothing", that means the markets are not responding, which means that the market is not being manipulated.
Could a "permanent" rate cut be an effective method of stimulating investment? If so, what would that look like? How would it affect investment, and what happens if the stimulus is temporary? Are there any signs that this would be a temporary stimulus? Or do people think the "stimulus" is permanent? 
A:

I've heard a lot of people say that there would not be any effect from a Fed Rate increase. But I don't think that is really true. 
There are two basic ways to stimulate an economy: one is through monetary policy (e.g. interest rate increases) and the other is by direct government action. If you had a country where the government was planning to increase its debt (which would give it a positive economic multiplier) but was not able to do so because of the debt ceiling, then you might say the economy is being stimulated. I think this is a mistake. The government can't directly stimulate the private sector. It can only raise taxes and/or reduce government spending. Both of these actions have the effect of increasing the money supply and thus the interest on the dollar. A stimulus for the US dollar is what the Federal Reserve does, through the open market operations. This is basically the same thing as saying that if you increase the supply of money, the value of your currency will rise. That is, if we increase money by increasing government debt then it will increase in value, but the increase is only due to the change in money (and the exchange rate is unaffected). This does not mean that all government actions are the equivalent of monetary stimulus. For example, taxes are taxes, so are spending cuts and increases in taxes. These are different actions. Some of them, like tax cuts, will have no effect on economic growth. Others, such as the spending cut in question, may have a measurable effect. However, I am not sure that a monetary increase would have an effect that would make the overall economy grow. And, as you suggest, there are other ways that stimulus could be used to improve the economic situation. Perhaps the best way to think of this, is that monetary and fiscal policy are separate.

Put options are a type of option with a strike price that is different than the underlying stock. These are often used when you want to hedge your exposure to the price of a stock, but don’t want the volatility of the stock to be reflected in your return. You could use put option contracts to buy a share of stock at a specific price, then sell that put when the value of that share increases or decreases.
There are several ways to do this. The simplest is to just buy the put, sell the call, and buy back the option when it expires. This is called a “straight put”. Another way to think about it is that you have a long put at the strike of one share, a short put that will expire at some future date, with no expiration date specified, called an “open put” or “O/E”. A call is just a call with an expiration time of zero, so it too can be thought of as an open put. If you buy open puts, the most important thing to remember is the expiration price. Don’ts: Don't buy puts that expire too soon, don't sell them that don' t expire, or don"t buy them at expiration. 
You can also buy options with different expiration dates. For example, you might want a put contract that gives you the right to sell a certain amount of shares when a specified time has passed, at any time. Or, if you're short a particular stock and need to time the market, buy an option to purchase a bunch of stocks at that price when certain conditions are met. In both cases, it's important to understand the difference between a straight put and a hedge. It's a common mistake to confuse the two, when in fact they are not the same. Hedge contracts are used to protect against a downturn in a market or an event that could make the contract worth less than its face value. They are usually in the form of an underlying asset, such as stock or bond, that has a higher price in one direction than in another. Put options have no underlying value and can't be hedged. To hedge a hedging contract, simply buy or sell put contracts when prices are higher than or lower than your target strike.

"Loss on inventory" is a common and popular way of describing items that have not been sold or exchanged for cash. "Losses on inventories" are a very specific type of "loss on books" that describes the total amount of inventory that has not yet been paid for. When inventory is not paid, the company has to pay the cost of keeping the inventory in order to keep it out of the "books". For example, if the department was keeping 25 cars, but only had enough to sell 4, it would need 4 cars to "keep the cars" and pay for the costs of storage.
The "costs of owning inventory", such as depreciation, repairs, and other expenses, are taken into account when calculating the amount the firm pays to acquire and store the items. The firm will also generally make a cash payment (deposit) to the client or other third party before it is able to get the item. This payment is commonly called "inventory funding".
If you have items on hand that are not in inventory, they are considered "unsaleable". This is often a part of a sales process that must be completed before the goods can be sold. For instance, you may have a bunch of unsaleables that you must collect before you can sell them. In this case, those items will be counted as inventory. They will never be paid as cash and will instead be used to cover the expenses incurred during the sale process, including depreciating the assets and paying for storage costs. If the sales department doesn't have enough money to buy the unsellables, then they will have to hire a third-party to collect them and then pay that thirdparty. These types of expenses are often referred to as "debt service", and the third parties are called the collector or the debt service department.

Equities are traded in the open market. ETF's are bought and sold in a closed market with very strict rules. The ETF rules tend to be more strict. Why? Because the ETF is a commodity that can be traded at the will of the issuer. That means it is very easy to manipulate, which is why the rules and regulations are so strict to make sure that there are no unfair trading. An ETF can have a lot of different investments, so there can't be a "one size fits all" approach. As a result, the investment decision is much more complicated. For this reason, ETF shares are generally more expensive than their counterparts in other asset classes, such as stocks. Also, because ETF funds are held in trust, they can only be bought by people who meet certain requirements. This makes it much harder for a company to buy up a large number of ETF holdings. Because of these reasons, it's not surprising that the share prices of an ETF are lower. They are also subject to more stringent rules because of this. Mutual funds, on the other hand, are open to anyone with a minimum investment amount. These funds can also be purchased by anyone, and a larger number can, too. But they are subject only to the same rules as the companies in which they invest. One of those rules is that mutual funds must be set up so that it does not lose money. When the fund does lose a certain amount of money, then the investors who hold the funds have to pay for it. (If they have no money to cover the loss, that loss is deducted from their investment. If they don't have money either, their money is returned.) If the company's stock does well, but it loses money on its investments (because of mismanagement, or because the people in charge of running the business have bad ideas), then they must pay the losses. In determining the amount of the partnership interest, the limited partner must use the formula below. The capital contribution made by each limited partnership must be added to the total capital of all partners.
The capital total of each partner is then multiplied by the number of limited partners, yielding the capital value of that partner. The value is multiplied across the partners to produce the gross partnership value. 
Note: the calculation of a partner's capital percentage is done in relation to their contribution to total partnership capital, not their individual contributions to that capital. This means that in the example below, a limited-partnership partner with a contribution of $100,000 would be considered a 30% limited, but not a 100% partner, because their capital would only be $30,100. 
For example, in a partnership with four limited partnerships, each of which has an annual gross value equal to $1,200, total gross capital is $4,400. Partner A contributed $200 to capital and partner B contributed 50% of capital ($200 ×.5 = $300). Partner C contributed 15% ($300 × 0.15 =$ 15), and finally, partner D contributed the remaining 10% (15% × $0.10 = 5). In this case, partners A, B, C, and D are all 30%, and they are called 30%.
If a general partner makes a $150, 000 contribution, which is 30 percent of total combined partnership assets, they would have a capital interest of 30/150 = 10%. It would not be called a 10%, but rather a 20% general partnership.

A tax is a law which regulates a person or a company. The tax can be imposed for a variety of reasons, including for example, to prevent and deter tax evasion.
State tax laws can also be classified as either general or specific. A state can levy a tax on a specific type of activity, such as a manufacturing activity. Such a state tax may be called a product tax. Alternatively, a general state law can impose a flat tax, which is assessed on all types of property and activities. This is often referred to as an excise tax or tax upon transactions. States can classify their general tax law into three broad categories:
Specific taxes that are imposed only on specific types or kinds of products or transactions or only for specific purposes;
General taxes, that apply to any type or kind of transaction or any purpose; and Excise taxes (also known as tax exemptions), that exempt only a particular type, kind or purpose of operation. For example: a manufacturer could be exempt from a sales tax by proving that he had no taxable income. However, if he were to sell taxable goods to a retailer, he would be liable to pay sales taxes. Some states classify excises as general taxes in order to facilitate the collection of revenue from businesses and other entities that have no state-specific tax liability. These general excisable taxes are often called indirect taxes because they are levied on an entity's activities, rather than on its assets. Examples of general, nontaxable excisers include: sales, interest, dividends, royalties, and rents. Taxation of nonresident individuals and corporations is generally a matter of state and not federal law. If a non resident individual or corporation has income or assets in another state, or the United States, the state or federal government will determine the tax consequences. In some cases, however, there may also have been a federal tax treaty.

The Blue line is an indicator used to indicate the top and bottom of the range that is being measured. It is used in the same way as the average.
What does the "range" mean? Simply, it is a range of points that are being calculated. The Blue lines are just the points in between the averages. They are not the actual average value, but they are the lowest and highest points of an average calculation. Since the Average is calculated based on a lot of averages, the lower and higher values of one average are also being used as a Blue range. This is why there are a few Blue values in an Average calculation that aren't necessarily the highest and lowest points. For example, in a 5-day Average, there could be a couple of Blue ranges, one that the 5th day and another that would be the 10th. As you can see, this is very helpful for the Stock Chart viewer in determining the exact range a stock should be in. If a Stock is at a certain Blue Range, then it probably is in that range for that day. However, if it's at the high or low end of that Blue Ranges, a different Stock might be better than that Stock for a specific day or period of time. Remember that it doesn't have to be at one particular Blue Value. In fact, you could have a low or high Blue value for one day, and then the next day that same Blue Stock could fall back to the normal range range, which is not necessarily at that low and high value. By keeping track of these ranges and their corresponding Blue Values, we can be sure that we are dealing with a good Stock.

In other words, the value is the difference between the account balance and the amount of money you could potentially earn if you sold the stock or bond. If the margin on the position was 100%, the broker could make a 1% profit on each $1 in the sale. This is known as a 100% leverage position.
On a 50/50 margin, if the buyer sold a stock for $10,000 and you bought it for the same price, you would lose $0.50. On a 20/80 margin you lose 20% of the original investment. That's a 2% loss. When you combine the two, a 5% margin is a $5 loss per $1000 of invested capital. A 10% broker margin would be a loss of $15 per thousand. The closer your margin percentage is to 100 percent, or the closer you can get to a pure buy/sell, your account will have a higher value. (The amount you make on a buy is called the "buy-back".)
If you sell a security and your buyer buys it at the market price and then sells it to you for a lower price than the initial purchase, in addition to the buy-out cost, there is an additional $2 in additional income. There are three basic ways to differentiate between a "gift" and a non-gift, depending on the circumstances. The first, and simplest, is to compare the intent of both the donor and the receiver. If they're not on first-name terms, if they don't have a business relationship, or if it was a small gift, the "intent" of gift-giving is irrelevant. But if you're trying to decide between gifts and payments, these are the only circumstances in which the other party's intent matters. So: Gift, when the party being given the donation is in a relationship with the giver; Gift or Payment, otherwise. 
You might also want to consider what the parties to the transaction are likely to think is fair, though this is less relevant to whether the thing is paid or a donation. For example, a company might give a $100 gift card to a person who works there, in exchange for a job, but to someone who does not work there. What is insider trading? Is it illegal in the UK? How does a person know if they are an insider? Can you be an “insider” in a company you work for? You may think this is a silly question, but some people don’t know the answer.
An insider is someone who has inside information about a firm that can be used to trade on their behalf. For example, if you know that a certain deal is going to happen, then you can trade that information for a price, with the help of your friends. There are also people who simply trade information with their friends about what is happening in their companies. An insider trader is one who trades information to the benefit of their company. This is also known as trading on inside knowledge. If you are trading information in this way, it is illegal. You could be violating the Trading on the Inside of Companies Act of 2006. The act states that it’s illegal to “trade on any information concerning a security that has been, or that may be, acquired by, disclosed to, given to or disclosed by the trader.”
So is it OK to be a trader if I know what a deal will happen? No, you cannot trade directly for the information. It is not legal to use inside info to make a trade. However, the insider in question may not know this. Someone could have made an inside trade and the company did not see it. In that case, they could technically be guilty of insider information trading, although this may or may never be proven in court. But this does not change the fact that you could never use this insider knowledge to your benefit. Trading is always risky. Some people are more likely to do this than others. Just like anything else, people have different levels of risk tolerance. A person with a higher level of tolerance will have less problems trading for information than someone with less tolerance because of how much information they have. So, when you ask someone to help you trade, try to find someone that is willing to give you some information and then find a way to turn it into a profit for you. Most people will be glad to lend a helping hand.

The Leveraged Inflations Hedge provides investors with a simple yet powerful tool to reduce the volatility of their investment portfolio. The Leverag Hedged portfolio is a leveraged portfolio that consists of a mix of fixed income, stocks and commodities. Leveraging can be used to increase the yield of the portfolio by purchasing bonds that are higher yielding than stocks or commodities and selling stocks that have the same or lower yields.
In addition to the leveraging effect, the Levered Inflated Held also reduces the risk associated with the inflation hedge. This risk can also be reduced by using the leverage to purchase a bond that is below the price of its maturity. By purchasing a below-market bond, investors are essentially locking in the value of this bond for the duration of that bond’s life. As the market values the bond at its price, it will be worth more than the amount invested. During the period of time that the investor holds the investment, they will receive the difference between the face value and the current market value. However, if the underlying bond is purchased at the wrong time, this loss can potentially be very large. To avoid this, an investor can purchase the above-average bond and hold it for a period longer than that of which it is expected to deliver. At the end of such a time period, when the original value is realized, a portion of it can then be redeemed by selling the below market bond. When purchasing the fixed-income bond or the stock, leverage is used on the opposite side of each asset class. For fixed interest, one can buy a high yield bond with leverage and sell a low-yield bond to lock in a positive return. Similarly, for stocks, levered portfolios can increase returns by buying low yielding stocks with little or no risk of loss and then selling those stocks at a premium.

When the company buys a security, they are selling the right to receive dividends from the underlying stock. This is called "security ownership." The term "securities" generally refers to anything that is the source of the income that the investor receives.
The term can also refer to the common stock of a company (see "common stock" below).
An investor can own all three types of assets, but a common investor will typically own the securities and the stock (or the preferred stock). The common shares are then sold to a public company. The investor then receives dividends (and other distributions) from both the stocks and from any preferred shares owned. An investor might not own any of these assets. If the individual is a pensioner, he or she might be entitled to some of this income, and then to be paid out in dividends. In that case, the pensioners' interests will be represented by the shares of stock or the assets in the portfolio. To illustrate this, let's say a retiree receives $50,000 a year in pension income. Her $5,500 in stock may be worth $15,750, or $10,250. For a typical investor, this is what they would own. They might buy some stock, as an example. But it might also be considered part of their portfolio, which they might own in their own name. Note that this example is more hypothetical than real, because it doesn't include the tax consequences of owning the two assets combined. It also doesn’t include any income to retirees who have the option of buying their assets from other people in order to get a tax break. However, it illustrates the basic idea. 
If a person buys an asset, such as a property, then that person owns a piece of that asset. That person can sell that piece, either to another person or to someone else who is not a party to that contract (i.e. a stranger). In the case of an individual buying a portfolio of stocks, that individual will own a portion of each of those stocks. Some of them will belong to an investor and some will not. So, if the person invests in a lot of shares, each share is owned by someone. Similarly, when the retire receives a payment from a government, some portion is actually owned in name by a private party. What the government is purchasing is "liability insurance."

“I am in my early 50s. I have a comfortable retirement income of $20,000/year. Assuming that I do not need to work in the next 10 years, what is the best way to spend my retirement savings?”
This is a good question. First, let me emphasize that your financial future does not depend on your current age. Your current financial situation is dependent on how much you earn over the years. If you need more income in retirement than you currently earn, you may need some help from your employer in that regard.
If you are not working in 10 or 20 years and you have $10,500/yr, the answer is that you would likely have to save about $3,600/month, for a 20% glider, to be able to afford your retirement. Let me try to break it down into two parts: the first part is for the current month and the second part for 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70 years into the future. Here is how I think the numbers break down: If your income over those 10-year periods is $5,800, then you will be saving an additional $1,700/mo. for retirement, if you do the gliding. 
I do this calculation by assuming that the income will stay at this level for 20 more years (this is just an example). If it does change, I would change the number. The total number of years is irrelevant. This is merely an estimate. So, your total spending for your future retirement is: $19,200/20yrs. Now, how to divide this number in two? In the past, when I looked at these questions, it was assumed that each person had a different retirement saving rate. What I did is calculate how many years it would take to reach that 20-30 year retirement (which is what most people are talking about when they say they want to retire early). I then divided that by the amount of money you want saved. In this case, that is 20k/30y. Then, divide that number by 20 (for the month) and by 30 (years) to get the percentage you should save. In the euro hedge funds world, you can find funds that offer two different products, i.e. index fund and single stock fund, or index option and equity fund. You can think of these funds as “passive” and “active” funds. In the passive funds, the managers of the fund will buy and sell index futures as well as the underlying securities. When you buy a fund with index options, then you’ll be buying a derivative of an index (i. e. the index is represented by a call option, a put option or a combination of both). For example, if you bought a 1.5% index call, in case you sell the option you will get 1/4 of 1% of its value. If you want to buy an equity index, for example the FTSE 100 index index or the Dow Jones Industrial Average, and want that to be your single asset, that’s not possible. The fund manager will have to sell a large portion of his portfolio (say 90% or more), and buy the same amount of a new portfolio, which contains the new index. That is why we say “index hedging” as it is a “hedge” in the sense that a manager of this fund (called the “manager”) is hedges his position. It is the manager’ s responsibility to select the appropriate securities and manage the position accordingly.
The index hedge fund has a unique characteristic: the portfolio manager is not a trader. He is only a passive investor. This means that the risk for the hedge is taken by the market. And that means the price of index hedgers is determined by what the traders are willing to pay for it. The reason for keeping separate accounts is so that the salary can be managed separately from the savings. This means that when you add money to the account you should do it on a separate transaction.
To clarify, this is a bit of an oversimplification. If you have an investment account where you put money in and keep it until you withdraw, then you are in effect investing in that account. 
So if you were to invest £1,000 in an account, you would have to be careful to not withdraw it in the same year as withdrawing £1000. So you can't do a withdrawal of £100 in one year and then invest the £200 the next year. Instead you need to transfer the money from your investment to your savings (so it is not actually invested in your portfolio, it's just "deposited" in a savings or pension fund).
If you want to make it easier for yourself to manage your money you could set up an individual savings plan (eg a Roth). This allows you to save money and use it when it suits you (ie you decide you don't need it, so you stop putting money into it). Then you set it up so it can only be withdrawn when required (say once a year). You can then transfer that money out of your current savings and deposit it into your new savings that you're using for your regular spending. 
As an aside, there is another reason that I think it makes sense to set separate savings accounts. That is to ensure that there are no tax consequences when the income from both your salary and your investments (in the case of the pension) is combined. In other words, if your pension and salary are combined, your contributions are not counted as income when calculating your taxable income. However, when one is taxed as a single entity, the other is counted separately.

If your yield isn’t great, then you are more hesitant to put your money into a home and wait for it to go up in value. You’d rather work with the property longer to see it appreciate in price than risk losing it. So it’’important to have enough yield for a reasonable amount of time to get your cash out. This is a common phenomenon.
When a company has a large amount of cash on hand, it has an incentive to use the cash to buy back stock. This is known as a “downdraft.” As a result, the stock price usually drops. So what happens when the company buys back the shares? It lowers the price of the whole stock and, as part of that, lowers its dividend. It’s a kind of “double-dip.”
The question is, when do you think a business is in a cash position and when is it a good time to sell? This depends on a number of factors, including what the business does and how it performs, how much cash it can afford to have on its balance sheet, and its ability to repay debt. You also have to consider the value of its assets, which is often not as stable as its liabilities. (See the chart below.)
To better understand what’ll happen when a firm buys or sells stock, here’re some more numbers:
 It typically takes about 12 months for a dividend to be paid on an average $1,000 of stock (or about 4 years on $100, if the dividend is paid quarterly).
You can’t buy a lot of shares in one day or month. That would be a short-term investment. In general, you’d have a much better chance of finding a buyer with more money, with the potential to make a better return. Think of it as buying when there’r a glut of stocks. But you don’ t have the same potential for long-run growth if you buy in the middle of a bull market. There’ s a reason for that. When you own a share of an industry leader, your company is more likely to survive a downturn, because it’ r better positioned to get back on track. The same is true of other businesses you might own, such as utilities, or healthcare stocks, where the industry is healthy. However, for stocks that aren’ re struggling, a dip could be the last straw. A dip is actually a sign that a market is overheated and that you should sell. If you're considering withdrawing from your Roth IRAs, you may find it useful to review your plan documents. You can usually find the details in the Summary Plan Description, which is contained in your IRA account statement.
There are a few things to consider. First, if you have the option of withdrawing funds from the Roth, that is probably the best option for you. If you aren't able to do so, the IRS may consider your retirement plan a "qualified trust," which will make your withdrawal taxable. And you'll probably want to be sure you fully understand the potential tax consequences of your choice. Second, keep in mind that you can withdraw funds up to the amount you deposited in IRA accounts. This means that if your contributions to your IRD fund are not as high as you might think, there's a chance you won't be able withdraw any money. Third, consider the possibility that the plan you use might not be available to you at retirement. For example, a 401(k) plan might be unavailable to retirees who have made contributions, or a retirement savings account might have a different withdrawal eligibility from a Roth account. Fourth, although the tax treatment of Roth contributions is generally favorable to retirement plans, it's not always so. There are tax rules that govern withdrawals from qualified retirement accounts, and the rules can vary depending on the type of account you are withdrawing. There is a difference between buying a stock on a dip and buying it outright.
On a dime, a buyer of a security will buy the stock and hold it until the next ding. For example, if a company is trading at $0.90 and the trade is made, the buyer will hold the security until it hits $1.00. 
When the market is at a high, they sell the entire position (or all the shares they own) immediately and get paid for their investment. On the other hand, when the markets are at their lowest, most investors do not have the patience to hold a position for too long, and sell out at the lowest bid. These two extremes are called a "bounce and a sale". A buyer buys the company and holds it for a while until they are able to buy it and then they begin to sell it. When the price goes up, their position is worth more and they will sell. The buyer who holds the position has a better chance to profit from the move up. If the dip is large, it may not be a good idea to invest in the whole position. This is because the upside will not keep pace with the drop. Therefore, some investors may decide to exit the investment before the bottom. So, buying on the dope is generally a bad idea.

The answer is no. If an investor cannot sell the option contract because of a lack of trading volume, it makes no difference if the investor has a long or short position.
When an option trader has an outstanding contract, he will receive a dividend, but the dividend will be less than the cost of exercising the contract. The exercise price may be higher or lower than what the trader had paid to buy the stock, depending on the strike price. In this case, the price difference is a loss to the seller. This is what is called a “market price” loss. But the net effect is the same. A long position results in a reduction of value, and a short puts in an increase of values. Thus, there is always a price loss, no matter what happens to market values, although the effect may not be immediate. It is this price drop that may result in the loss of investor capital. To avoid this loss in value to be eliminated, an exchange offers a market price risk premium, which is an amount to cover this market value loss for a fixed time period. By investing in this premium and selling the underlying stock when the premium is earned, a trader can offset the market loss and avoid a potential loss on his investment. Therefore, if an options trader cannot hold his long stock because the volume is not sufficient, then he should sell his options and buy an underlying security at a higher price (e.g., the current market index).
Another option for the long investor is to sell short and hold the position for an extended period of time, hoping that the trend will turn around and the volatility will return. Of course, this is risky and, in general, not recommended. Another method for long investors is by selling short for cash. There are numerous short selling programs on Wall Street and in private equity funds, where funds can borrow against their shares and sell them short to take advantage of low prices.

A bonus is tax deductible for any taxable year. The tax treatment depends on how the bonus was earned.
If the employee was granted a salary during the year, the salary will be treated as a tax deduction. If the bonuses were earned in the tax years before the grant, they will not be deducted. For example, a year-end bonus in a current year is not deductable in 2018. However, if the company gave the employees a one-time bonus, it will still be considered a deduction for 2018, despite the fact that the actual amount was not earned until after the end of the current tax period. In the above example a 2018 one time bonus would not reduce the 2018 tax liability. On the other hand, tax-free distributions of unused salary would reduce 2018 income tax. This is because they are treated in 2016 as an increase in salary for the purposes of calculating the 2017 tax bracket. So, 2018 bonus distributions will reduce income taxes on the distribution for 2017, but will increase income for 2016. It is important to note that any tax deductions on distributions are subject to a 50% reduction if they were made within the last three years. Generally, when an employee receives a payment of more than $3,000 for an item such as rent, utilities, or food, this is treated like a taxable distribution. When the payment is less than the amount required to reduce an income-tax deduction, there is a 25% tax penalty. There is also a 10% penalty when the employer pays the entire amount, and there will also be a 20% deduction on any other item paid to the taxpayer.

Yes, you are required to report your business income and expenses for the year in which you file your 1040.
If you have a business in your home state and you want to file a 1099, your state’s FICA and Medicare taxes will be reported to the IRS. However, if you do not have any business activity in the state, then you will not be required by the FASB to submit the 1095 to your employer. If you don’t have an employer, and your sole business is a sole proprietorship, or you own your own home and are self-employed, it is not required that you report business expenses on Schedule C. You are still required, however, to keep records of your trade or business. The FTA and FDC’S will look at your Schedule D to verify that your income is reported on a Schedule A. Schedule B is your “Schedule C.”
Remember, the last time you filed a return was when you first became self employed. But if your self employment ended before you were required or permitted to make the return, that’ll be the first return you can file. Therefore, even though you may have filed an old return before, unless you got some sort of approval for an amended return (e.g., an amendment to a prior return that allows for more deductions, more business deductions or a reduction in business losses), you still have to return the old one. It’d be a good idea to contact the tax preparer you use for your return preparation. She may be able to help you with this issue. I would also like to point out that filing your tax returns online is much easier than filing them in paper. This way you only have one form to fill out. Check the US Treasury website for information on how to do this.

At this point, it’s important to understand what these figures mean.
First, the 10-year note is not a single benchmark. Instead, each 10 year note represents the performance of an individual investment (see the chart below).
The 10 Year Treasury Note is the average of the ten most recent annualized returns. The numbers shown above are the returns for ten of these ten-yr. notes. As the number of notes in the portfolio increases, so does the total return. For example, if you have 10,000 shares of a stock, and you sell 500 of them each year, you’d have a portfolio with 10 years of returns of roughly 3%. If you had 10 million shares, your portfolio would have ten years worth of 10% returns, or roughly 9%.
In the same way, a 10 yr. Treasury note from the 30-Year Treasury bond is a performance based on the past 30 years. So if the bond yields were the only variable in your model, then the current 10 Yr. note would be the best choice. However, we can also think of it as a 30 year investment with a ten year maturity. This is what a Treasury Inflation Protected Securities is, which would represent the most efficient and risk-free investment for you. In reality, most investors are trading stocks that are more volatile. To minimize risk, this model uses a different risk measurement and is used as an inflation hedge. There is no inflation protection when buying this note. You would still need to buy stocks, but this is much less risky than buying a note with inflation. (Note: a “TIPS” is also a form of inflation protected note.)
There is one note that is considered a benchmark for comparison. It’ s the benchmark 10yr Treasury Bond. If the yield on that note were to rise, that would affect the value of all the other 10YR notes, as well. But if it were not to go up, all other notes would return to their previous levels. Therefore, even though the note isn’t the ultimate measure of risk (because it doesn’ t include inflation), it still provides the closest comparison to other investments.

I would like to clarify some terminology used in this article.
When we talk about a "bullish" signal we are talking about an indicator that signals a strong bearish reversal. We are not talking here about the "sell signal" in the sense of a sell signal that is used to signal a bear market. A "buy signal", as it is called in the financial community, is a signal to buy a particular stock. In other words, it is a strong buy signal. This is an important distinction. The term "bearish sell" does not indicate an opposite of "strong buy". It is merely a term for a sell that the analysts use to indicate a reversal of the previous strong sell. It would not be called a buy for every strong "b" sell because it would be a bad signal in some cases. An example of a bullish signal is the following:
"The RSI is above the midpoint and the MACD is below the zero line. If the Rsi is above the 0 line, then this signal indicates that a trend reversal is likely."
On the other hand, a trader might call a stock a low "l" buy if the price is lower than $30 and a high "h" "high" if it exceeds $50. These signals are a little different because they are bear signals. They would signal strong bear markets and would also signal reversal signals in other cases. That is why they will be used differently. And one more important point is that these signals can be positive or negative. On the one hand, an "overbought" market could be considered bear, whereas a market that exceeds its 200 day moving average might be bull. But in both cases, the signals have to be strong.

When you invest in an exchange-traded fund (ETF), you buy shares in a company and then you can sell them to someone else. The shares you purchase are then held in trust by a custodian company. Once you decide you no longer need the shares, you sell the ETF.
The ETF investor can then reinvest the dividends it receives and reinstate the original shares. This is known as reinventing dividends. If the dividend reinvention rate is higher than the investment return on the underlying stock, the reinstituted shares will be worth more than they were in the company when the investor purchased them. In other words, reinventions are a way for investors to earn a higher return than by investing in shares of the same company directly. Since the stock price of ETFs is often less volatile than that of their underlying stocks, this means reinstitutions could add more value than investing directly in stock. However, most ETF investors are not concerned with reinstitution rates, and instead, they are concerned about reinstituting dividends received. For example, if a stock has a reinjection rate of 7.5% and the market price is $10,000, then an investor who reinjects $1,500 would earn $7,750 in return. Conversely, an investment of $500 that reinjected $100 would return $5,625. These reinfections are what investors pay attention to. When reinclusions are high, investors will pay more for the stocks they hold. On the other hand, when reinclations are low, it makes sense to hold a few shares to reinstitute dividends, rather than a large number of shares for reinceptions. Therefore, ETF's reinclusion rates tend to be low. There are many other factors involved in ETF prices and their reinformance rates. ETF stocks usually have low reinclude rates because the return is so low that it's worth reincluding dividends that have already been reinjured. Another reason for lower reinclusive rates is that ETF shares are often purchased and held for a longer time than shares held by investors who invest directly through an individual stock broker. Thus, some ETF companies might have high reinception rates to reduce their costs.

text:
Investors can potentially lose a lot of money by taking a position in bonds.
If you’re not careful, the bond might actually be worth less than you thought. Here’s how it works:
As bonds mature, they are typically paid off over time. The higher the interest rates,
the more the bonds are worth, and the less the investors will be required to pay. But what happens when the yield of bonds falls? The lower the rate of return, so the earlier the maturity date, that’ll be the more expensive the investment. If bond yields fall below the investor’ preferred interest level, then the value of the debt might actually decrease. That’d make it less appealing to own and invest in bond. Bonds are also subject to inflation. So if the inflation rate is higher than the prevailing interest rate, investors could end up paying more in interest and principal each year. All of these factors could lead to a lower return on the principal invested. This is called bond risk. A bond that is paying a higher interest yield than investors expect could be rated as a riskier investment. You could lose money if you buy into a bond before it matures, or a higher-yield bond is purchased before maturity. When you invest, you can’t be sure whether the market price of a security will rise or fall. And the price you get for your bond could actually drop. There could also be a risk that the issuer of your bond could go bankrupt. Investors could have to take out a loan to buy the securities they purchased and that could get a little more costly if they default. For example, if a company is going to go out of business, it could take longer for investors to get their money back. In this case, bondholders might get stuck with a portion of their money. These are all risks and investors should understand that they can lose significant amounts of cash. To make matters worse, bonds can be risky even if interest rates are low. High inflation rates can cause bonds to lose value. As a result, even if bond yields are lower than current interest levels, some investors may not want to buy bonds with low yields. They might prefer bonds that are paying higher yields, which could lead them to end their investment in a particular bond earlier than expected.

I've got a pretty good job that pays pretty well. But I've been offered a position with a company that offers a generous 401K. The company matches my employer's match and there's a $10,000 match for me. So I figure I should participate.
Is this something I need to think about? If so, why? I'm not sure what to make of it. 
A:
Here's what I think. 
The 401(k) has a very simple structure. It's just a way of investing in mutual funds, exchange-traded funds and other investments. You are not contributing to your company's retirement plan. Your company may have a retirement savings plan, which may or may not match the 401 (if it has one), but it is not a part of the company retirement. In other words, it's not just the money that's being invested in the plan; it also has to be invested, but that is something you do with your own money. 
Your company is investing your money, and it can invest as much as it wants in its own plan or not invest at all. If it doesn't want to invest any money in your plan then it isn't participating in it at any point. Also, if you are contributing your employer matching 401 plan in any way then you're contributing the funds from that plan to the overall plan of your current employer. This is a big deal, because if your employee plan is contributing less than the employer plan (which it should be if they match), then they will be paying more than they should. That's how much money they are paying in taxes, too.

As the business grows and the shares of stock increase in value, more and more people start to own the equity of that company. They are called shareholders. If the value of shares rises so that the number of shareholders is increasing, then the share price must fall. This is what happens when an IPO is announced. Your question, like many others, has multiple layers of confusion and false assumptions.
The short answer is that a stock is a claim on the value of the business or assets, which the company can sell or use to pay dividends. The value the stock represents is how much the owner of that share would receive if the share was sold. 
Options, on its face, are a way to exercise a right to purchase a share in the future. Options are not a security and thus have no value. They are an option to buy shares in a company. The owner can exercise this right only if he owns a specific number of shares. In most cases, options have very limited appeal for their holder. This is because the holder has to wait for the right time to sell his shares (e.g. at a certain price or at the current market price) and if this time is not yet available, the option holder is stuck with the shares that he has. (It is also possible for an investor to be stuck holding shares for which he does not own any.)
In the case of options, it is the buyer who has the ability to decide when to take the options (or sell them) from the seller. If the price of a particular stock at some point becomes less than the strike price, then the potential buyer of an options contract can decide to have the contract cancelled. He can do this by paying a premium to cancel the agreement. So, by definition, there is no "stock" involved in an exercise of option rights. It is just the same as if a buyer had bought the underlying share at $25 and then sold it for $30 (assuming the market was at or above the $15 strike).
Another important thing to realize is when you are buying shares you do not get the actual shares themselves (which means you cannot exercise options). You get shares which have some rights in relation to those shares and which can be sold for cash. It's like a bank account. You can use it to pay a bill, but you shouldn't always use the money to buy more bills. The same idea applies to stocks. There is nothing wrong with buying more stocks than your current account balance, so long as you keep doing it over time. It will make you more money. But the same can be said about selling. A good rule of thumb is to sell your stock only if you're down to your last $5. (The reason is that the market is always going to be volatile. When you sell, the price will go down, and if the last 5 dollars you sold it were $25, then the next day it would be $20. That will cause you to lose money, because you'll have to replace your original stock at a lower price. So, if there is a $10 difference in the prices, your $0.25 loss is $2.50, which you need to make up by buying the stock again. This will be a losing situation for you.)
The key is not to rush. Buy it when you think the cost is reasonable, sell when it is high. And remember: you will always make more when the value of your investment increases over the course of a year. Not only will you have more cash, more free money for investing, a higher net worth and a better lifestyle, with less effort, time and money invested. In the long run, this will pay off handsomely. Most of the time when you are buying a house, you will need to borrow money to pay for it. But, the problem with this is that there is a good chance that the loan will be taken out by the borrower’s own bank. This means that you have to make sure that your property will remain in your name.
In the case of buying property using a loan, it is important to note that such loans do not have a mortgage clause which prevents your house from becoming your collateral. So, if you want to sell the property in the future, your bank will not be able to take any of your assets. You will have no other choice than to let your home go to foreclosure. What this means is, that if your lender comes knocking at your door with a foreclosure notice, they will first go through the house to get rid of anything that is not in their possession. If they find any money, then they can take it all from you. On the other hand, even if they do find money in a property, there will still be a chance of a short sale. In that case, instead of getting rid off the owner of that property by foreclosure, he will take a portion of it off you in exchange for the equity. Even though this sounds bad, this option is the only way that lenders will allow you to keep your family’ s home. Thus, in order to avoid being forced to give the lender everything, we have always advised our clients to use the cash collateral method to buy properties. With this method, a lender will only be given a percentage of what you owe on the sale of property. The rest of money is kept in an escrow account. When you sell, or refinance, property with cash, as collateral, and the buyer defaults, what happens? The bank takes the collateral and they get their money back. They do so by selling your title to the new buyer and then collecting the money that they paid you back for. Cash collateral is only a method for you if it suits your needs. It is just a way of protecting yourself from foreclosure and also keeping your cash at hand.

My main focus was on non employees, and not on shareholders, because the latter can still have their "share" valued in some way.

The way we are taught to think about lending money is that it is always a bad idea. But sometimes it’s the best idea for the person you are lending it to. There are two reasons why we can lend money, but not loan money.
First is the moral reason. We can’t lend our money back to someone. Lending is not the same as borrowing. The person is lending you money because they want to help you out financially, and not because you owe them money for something. If we lend someone money we have a responsibility to repay that money at the end of the loan. This is why loan companies are regulated, because if you can get a loan and then say I don’ t need your money anymore, then you’ve broken the law. (Lending money can be illegal, in fact, if the money you lend is used to buy drugs or alcohol or something like that.)
Second, there are some things you might lend to a friend or relative that are not suitable for loan, such as a car or home. Some loans are for very specific things like car repairs or a new roof, or some people might be able to get into debt themselves, so they don't need to borrow money from you. These are different situations, though, than the situation when you borrow from friends and family. So, when should you and your friends be on the lookout for ways to make sure you don t end up in a situation where you have to pay off the debt? Here are a few ideas:
Is the interest rate higher than your own? If it does, that could be a sign that the friend has a tendency to overpay for their car. Is the term length of time that you will be responsible for repaying the amount higher? This could also be an indicator that your relative is more likely to default on their loan than you would be. Also, check out whether there is any way that they can avoid repays on a certain date. For example, they could say that if your loan is paid off by August 31, you won’ get all your interest, including any interest you had to take on. Or, the reverse: if they repay their debt by January 31 they will get their interest back, as well as any fees or interest they had taken on for that period.

Risks in the short run are a function of the current level of risk and the probability that a business will fail.
The probability of a failure occurring is the result of many factors, including the business's ability to continue to meet its obligations under the contracts, its ability (or inability) to provide sufficient funds, and its capacity to repay its creditors. Each of these factors is affected by the level and nature of risks of all the businesses in a group. This means that the risk of one business in this group is a combination of its own and of other businesses' risks. The combined effect of this risk on the financial health of any business is called the aggregate risk. In the long run, the overall risk is determined by how well a company, or any number of companies, can withstand the combined risks that all companies in its group face. If one company or group of businesses can weather the storm, then the remaining companies and groups will be able to survive and prosper. However, if the group's survival depends on some other company's or groups' survival, it is likely that one or more of those companies will not survive. As a result, some companies or some groups of firms may be unable to weather some of their combined business risks, even though other firms or other groups may not be so exposed. So, how does the combination effect the total risk? To illustrate, we consider a one-industry group consisting of four firms. Suppose the one firm's aggregate exposure to the others' combined risk equals its current market value. We can see that this firm would be in no worse a position than if its market capitalization had been zero. It would therefore be unaffected by any reduction in capital stock. Your first question is answered in IRS Publication 463, “Revenue Procedure” (Rev. Proc. 2010-14). As you note, the law generally provides that amounts paid to a third party for goods or services are not deductible. If you have already paid the third-party for those goods and services, then the payment is a “direct payment,” and your itemized deductions will include the amount paid for the goods. The law provides a special rule for reimbursement for moving costs.
What is reimbursement? In the case of a business, if you pay for your own personal travel, you are reimbursed for that expense. This is called “reimbursement.” If your personal expenses are paid by another person, that is known as “contribution.” The IRS has the authority to require you to reimburse the other person for any expenses they paid you. Generally, however, a person who pays for personal business expenses, such as expenses for a moving company, is not required to pay any reimbursement to the person paying for such expenses. For example, let’s say you and a friend were to rent a storage unit for $400 a month. You do not have to make any payments to your friend. However, your rental expenses would be subject to income tax. Your friend would have his tax bill sent to you, and you would deduct your expenses on your return. (You would still pay the taxes, but your deductibility would not be affected.)
If you receive reimbursement, generally it is for up to 90% of the actual expenses you paid. A “reasonable allowance” is allowed in some circumstances. In this situation, there is no actual expense, so the “allowance” would relate to “amounts you reasonably could have spent” on the item. An example of this is when you buy a ticket for an airline flight and pay cash. Most airlines will reimbure you for this amount. Some airlines reimbute you only for actual costs, like a charge for baggage or a change of plane. It is up in the air for how much you can be reimbursable. Again, it depends on what you actually paid and how you spent it. There are also special rules for tax-exempt organizations, charities, certain nonprofit organizations (for example religious or social service organizations), and certain charitable organizations. See Publication 1412, IRS Revenue Procedure. Publication 1520 provides general rules about the tax treatment of reimbursements.

In 2006, the University of Chicago’s Center for the Study of Existential Risk and the Risk Society published a report that examined the impact of technology on individual and collective well-being. The report concluded that “the technology that we now use in the industrial economy is largely invisible to us—we have no way of knowing what it is doing to our lives and our environment.”
The report also noted that technology is changing us, and as a result, “we are changing technology” as well.
As technology becomes more powerful and pervasive, we are being asked to accept a more complex reality, a reality that is more unsettling, more stressful, less comfortable, with more opportunities to be unhappy. Technology can be a tool for self-management, but it can also be an “enabler.” That is, technology can provide the means to manage, manage better, or manage worse. We are learning to live with the consequences of our choices. It is a process that goes deeper than we can see or even know. The process of change is ongoing. Change is the result of the interaction of many forces, not just technology. But the change that will occur will be for better or worse, depending on how we manage it. As the report notes,
“It is difficult to predict the future with any certainty, even with technology’ own rapid progress. However, if we use the scientific approach to understanding the way technology changes and changes us as individuals and groups, then we may be able to make better decisions in our own lives as we face the challenges and opportunities of tomorrow.” 
This suggests that the only way to understand the process and impact that change will have on us is to use a scientific process to assess the potential consequences, as described in this book. That way, you can then make your own best guess as to how you will respond to that unknown future.

This is because the $5 gain is worth more to you if the stock trades at $110 than it would if trading at just $85. The difference is called price/earning. A stock with a higher PE would be a better investment if a market goes up, because it will pay a larger price for it. 
Another way to think of this is to compare the cost of owning a share of stock to the value of that share. Suppose we were to buy $10,000 worth of Apple stock at the current market price. Investment Risk is generally defined as the risk of loss in the total return of the investment portfolio. It is measured in terms of both the volatility and the magnitude of that volatility.
The volatility is the standard deviation of a portfolio’s return in a given period of time. For example, the return for a 30-year bond is a standard normal distribution, and its standard deviation is 1.5%. The volatility of return is defined by the square root of standard variance. In other words, if the expected return (return on investment) is 10% per year, then the variance (standard deviation) of expected returns is 3%.
As an example of how to measure the level of risk for an investment, consider a bond that has a maturity of 30 years and is yielding 2%. If the initial investment is $10,000 and after 30 days the value is only $9,900, there is an annual loss of $900. This is called a 20% annual return. If there were no volatility, this would be a 40% return, but since there was a volatility (20% yearly return) this is still a loss (40%).
A standard risk measure is also referred to as a “variance”. It can be calculated as
(R-P)/P,
where R is risk, P is return and R- is loss. So a risk measurement is simply the difference between the returns and it is expressed as either a percentage or as standard deviations (in units of percentage).
This calculation is different from the calculation for standard returns. Standard returns are calculated using the formula R=P/(1+r),
which is equivalent to the equation above. However, standard risks are typically calculated by multiplying the R by a factor of P. A factor is typically called the “premium”. The premium is calculated for any given type of bond or portfolio and can represent the amount of money that is needed to compensate for the risks that are associated with the bond. The higher the premium, for example 1%, the greater the loss that the investor will experience as compared to an investor that does not own the bonds.

When an investor in financial markets buys a call or puts, he gets a premium over his risk-free rate of return, plus interest on the premium paid. He is also taking on some risk of loss in the event of a default. If he buys more of the underlying stock, the risk is lessened.
If he hedges the stock position, then the amount of money he will lose is more than the extra risk he is taking. This is because he has sold the security at a price that is lower than his average risk. By holding the futures, instead of buying the shares, his losses are less. In the case of short term futures contracts, this is not the same as hedging the whole position. For example, if the market goes up, and his interest rate is 8%, he loses 8% more. This exception to the wash sale rules will apply only to a small number of individuals who are not able to make use of cash or card payments from their bank accounts and hence need to opt for cashless payment. The exception will only be for those who do not have a bank account and are forced to choose between getting cash from a store and using their debit or credit cards. Similarly, if a customer does not use cash at any store, then there will be no wash sales rule applicable to him. In the next scenario, a person with a personal loan or a mortgage is being financed by a lender through a loan agreement. If the loan amount exceeds the annual percentage rate (APR) of a borrower, it is called a ‘wash sale’. The washsale will impact the borrowers in the following ways:
 The borrow will have to pay a higher interest rate to repay the principal of his loan. The interest will remain unchanged on the interest charged on his repayment amount. Therefore, his interest payment will also remain the same. But, at the end of each month, he will get a larger amount of interest and a smaller amount in repayments. If interest rates are higher for a longer period of time, more interest is accrued on principal. For example, with an interest of 8% for five years, in five months of repay, interest would be accrued of eight percent. After five more months, only seven percent would remain. With an APR of 25%, the amount accrued for repay would only remain of seven per cent. Thus, after five additional months a repay of only four per cents would occur. These are the reasons why the lender or borrow can opt to wash the sale of their loan to avoid any increase in interest payments. It is also the reason that the lenders can choose to take a lower interest on loans to their borrow. As per the ABP rules of 2017, banks cannot offer a wash purchase to any borrow under ABRs of 5 per cen. Hence, this would not impact banks to offer this type of services.
